The Playful Sport of Kālahastīśa

Salutations to Śrī Devī; salutations to Śrī Kāla... I recognize the supreme excellence of that which belongs to Śaṅkara; therein, I bow to Your form which is... Indeed, who is this? It is said: "Brahman, Śa... He...
From worms and insects up to the gods,

[the world] proceeds as long as it is subject to the activity of the senses; nevertheless, because Brahman is the cause of transformation, and due to its connection with the state of being the progenitor,
the Supreme Person, the Supreme Lord, is distinct from that which consists of the transformation of the body and so forth.

Thus, from the context and the word "Brahman," it is understood that He alone is the one to be saluted, as in the passage: "He who is the Great Brahman, the Supreme Goal. That abode is to be meditated upon; for this term [Brahman] is not used figuratively, whereas elsewhere it is used figuratively.

If it is argued that the term *brahman* is seen to be applied even to generic categories, individual souls, and so forth— since the *Nighaṇṭu* states, "Those [are called] Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Bhagavat, [and] Prajāpati"— we say no; for there is no such lack of distinction [in those cases], just as the term *Īśvara* is applied [to various beings] through figurative usage (*yoga*).

Therefore, the term "Brahman" is used primarily for Nārāyaṇa; elsewhere it is used in a secondary sense. In Nārāyaṇa, the word is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*). Now, why is he called Brahman? Because he is "Great" (*bṛhan*) and because "in him all this is contained" (*asmin sarvam idam vartate*). Within the ocean, O God, he is endowed with all powers; such is the view of the wise.

The word "Brahman" is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) for Nārāyaṇa by the consensus of the learned; however, its conventional application to the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth is [merely] metaphorical (*yaugika*).

Because the strength of the established usage among the noble ones regarding the root of delusion has been cultivated, and because [the term] is established in words such as "barley" (*yava*) and "boar" (*varāha*), and because in the second view it possesses both etymological and conventional meaning (*yogarūḍhatva*) in Viṣṇu— just like the word "Viṣṇu"— there is no lack of probative force in the Śruti.

Regarding the alleged futility of its etymological derivation (*tannirvacanavaiyarthyam*), it is said here: although the word "Brahman" and the word "Lord" (*bhagavat*) [are established] as primarily denoting Viṣṇu through the example [of other terms], this does not preclude the fact that words such as "cow" (*go*), which possess multiple meanings, apply to all their respective referents, such as heaven and so forth, in accordance with their semantic range.

By virtue of its primary sense, [the word] ought to be primary only with respect to an individual possessing a dewlap and so forth, based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that which goes (*gacchati*) is a cow (*goḥ*). Alternatively, the word becomes primary in relation to the [genus] *bhū*. [This is because] the *Nighaṇṭu* establishes that it has multiple meanings.
Because of contradiction; otherwise, there would be a plurality of meanings [regarding] the perishable and the imperishable in the scripture.

Furthermore, Viṣṇu’s status as the creator is stated by virtue of his primacy. Just as [qualities arise] according to proximity, so too does he manifest in an unmanifest form; likewise, Viṣṇu is the Lord of all.

It is so recorded. Here, because the term "Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara*) describes the state of being subject to agitation through forms such as contraction and expansion, there is no contradiction between those two [states].
Furthermore, since it establishes a secondary creation performed by Nārāyaṇa, Nārāyaṇa is [the agent].

There is a contradiction. Regarding its manifestation... [the Supreme Lord] consists of Brahman, is identical with the universe, all-pervading, the Lord of all beings, the Self of all, and the Supreme Lord. This is because Pradhāna lacks the sovereignty that is the cause for such activity and the absence of [such] lordship.
Because it is not established as having multiple meanings, like the word *brahman* (p. 4). [Objection: But how [is this so] on the basis of the *Nighaṇṭu*?

[Objection: There is no validity for determining the meaning of the Veda [based on human treatises], because they are of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). [Reply: Even that which is of human origin possesses validity, like the *smṛti* (traditional law), insofar as it serves to remind one of beginningless usage—as in the case of such [Vedic injunctions] as "One should sacrifice a *pika*."

Furthermore, it is stated that even the usage by non-Aryans (*anārya*) is useful for determining the meaning of a sentence. Now, one might object: "In the case of conventional terms (*rūḍha*) such as *pika*, since there is no usage by Aryans, the usage by non-Aryans is the determinant; however, in the case of the word *brahman*, like the word *yava* and others, the usage by Aryans is the determinant. This is not so.

Since the authors of the *Nighaṇṭu* were experts in grammar and other sciences, [their usage] exists even in cases such as generic classes (*jāti*). Therefore, when there is a contradiction between the linguistic conventions of the Āryas and the Anāryas regarding different domains, no [conflict arises] therein; for in this case, that [contradiction] is absent. [Ave...]

If it is argued that there is an absence of a basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) regarding the word [Brahman], [we reply] that this is not so; for in the case of the syllable *praṇava* (Om), in the phrase "O Brahman," and in the case of the four-faced one (Brahmā) and others, it is impossible to state a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) that is co-extensive with them. [The root is] *bṛh* (to grow/great).

Regarding the term "vṛddhau" (in the two elders): because the universal *brāhmaṇatva* (brahminhood) is not perceived in [the individual] elders, it is impossible for it to be the delimiter of the denotatum (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).
Due to parsimony (*lāghava*), it is the universal *brāhmaṇatva* itself [that serves as the delimiter].
Furthermore, if that which is other than the meaning of the individual parts— which serves as the ground for the application [of the word]— is not cognized from the word itself,
yet is still held to be the delimitor of the denotable object (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), then it would be possible to say the same regarding words such as *aśva* (horse) or *go* (cow);
consequently, the category of polysemous words (*nānārtha*) would be abolished.
In reality, however, [the question arises]: "Why is she called Tārā? Why is she called Praṇava? And why is she called Brahman?"—as found in the sections concerning the Praṇava. (p. 5)

In the context of questions and answers, by taking recourse to the relationship of non-difference (*abheda*) between the signified and the signifier, the unsurpassed Brahman-hood existing in the Supreme Lord, the Parabrahman, is superimposed upon the *praṇava*;
thus, it becomes figurative (*gauṇa*). In reality, however, in the *Atharva-upaniṣad*, it is said: "The gods, indeed, [went] to heaven..."
They went to the world. They asked Rudra: "Who are you? He replied: "I alone existed in the beginning, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future. There is no one else whatsoever distinct from me.
Having begun thus, it continues: "The gods meditated upon Rudra," and in the middle [it says] "the supreme..."

Because it is determined that the passage refers exclusively to Rudra through the concluding statement, "Reflecting thus, one should chant this deed of Rudra," which forms a single syntactical unit; and because the term "Brahman" is employed as a synonym for that [Rudra] by superimposing the identity of Brahman upon the *praṇava*— which has been established as a means for his worship— in order to praise it, using the word "Brahman" which denotes him.

Regarding the term "nirdeśa" (designation): the word *brahman* is primary when applied to Rudra, and because it is superimposed as non-different from him, it is likewise primary when applied to the *praṇava* (Om). Otherwise, even the word *hari* would be secondary when applied to a frog or a monkey.

Furthermore, inference is also untenable; for if one were to attempt to prove that [the word] is primary in relation to Viṣṇu, it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

In that very same proof for primacy (*mukhyatva*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the term "Hari. Likewise, the view that [the word] possesses both etymological and conventional meaning (*yogarūḍhi*) should be understood as refuted; for, due to the absence of the constituent parts of the word "Brahman" and because of the aforementioned deviation, its status as etymological (*yaugika*)—in the sense of denoting the fullness of qualities—is not established.

Because, through the possibility [of etymological derivation], the status of being both etymological (*yogika*) and conventional (*rūḍha*) is established even for the word "Brahman. For this is not the case with the etymological word "cow" (*dhenu*), nor with the conventionally etymological word "lotus" (*paṅkaja*).
No one has accepted that a word possesses an etymological (*yaugika*) meaning by taking an object that transcends the meanings of its constituent parts (*avayava*).

If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of the Vedic text, 'For great indeed are the qualities in him'? we reply that it is merely a figurative construction (*kalpita*). Even if it were not a figurative construction, it would be a transfer of designation (*atideśa*) based on a mere similarity of attributes (*dharma-mātra*).

Because, like a sentence, it serves merely to apprehend the capacity [of the word], the "greatness of qualities" (bṛhadguṇatva) which is its referent cannot be the delimitor of the denotable meaning (śakyatāvacchedaka). Furthermore, it is observed that when a Southerner asks, "What kind of creature is a camel? in response to a comparison based solely on its property [of being large], the answer given is "It has a long neck."

Because the meaning of the sentence "The animal that has long lips, eats thorns, and urinates [in such a manner]" lacks the status of being the delimitor of the denotatum (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), it serves as an auxiliary factor in the apprehension of the word's primary power (*śaktigraha*).

If it is argued that "in that case [the word 'camel'], camel-ness (*uṣṭratva*) exists as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), whereas this is not so for the word 'Brahman'," we reply: no; for in the case of the word ['Brahman'], there is the possibility of various properties—such as vastness (*bṛhattva*) cognized from the word itself, or Brahminhood (*brahmaṇatva*), and so on—serving as the delimiters of denotability.

Because there is no evidence for the status of "fullness" (*pūrṇatva*) as a qualifier when it is not cognized from the word itself. If it is argued that "conventional usage" (*rūḍhi*) alone should suffice, we say no; because there is an absence of a cognition having "Viṣṇu-ness" as its qualifier, there is an absence of a power delimited by that [qualifier]. [Jñā...]

It has also been refuted that the *Kalpasūtras* determine the meaning of the term "Brahman," because there is no evidence for their authority in establishing non-difference or in determining the primary denotation (*śakti*) [of the word]. That very point...

Furthermore, the phrase "Brahman is the supreme among the poets" does not establish a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*). Just as when it is said that for a king endowed with qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the supreme duty (*paramo dharma*) is the protection of his subjects,
it is understood that protection alone is the primary meaning of the word "duty" (*dharma*), while its definition as being characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*) is secondary.

It is not logical to say that [the term] is primary. When it is said, "Caitra is supremely righteous," although Caitra is superior by virtue of his righteousness, it is not logical for the word "righteous" (dhārmika) to be secondary with respect to one who performs sacrifices and the like, while being primary with respect to Caitra. Otherwise, [it would lead to an absurdity].

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the term "supreme state" being rendered meaningless. For it is only when [the Supreme Being] is common with Brahman that the term "supreme state" becomes meaningful.
By this it is established that Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman, as stated in the Bhārata: "The Supreme is that which is the Great Brahman."
The statement has also been explained. Since in the *Gītā* Nārāyaṇa designates himself as distinct from Brahman, even there the primary application of the term "Brahman" to himself is precluded.
And it is said: "What is that Brahman? What is the inner self (*adhyātma*)? What is action, O Supreme Person? and so forth.

In response to the questions posed by Arjuna, the Blessed One gave an answer beginning with "The Imperishable is the supreme Brahman" and ending with "I alone am the sacrifice. In that context, if He Himself were the Supreme Brahman, He would have said, "I alone am the Supreme Brahman."
Just as it is said, "I alone am the Adhiyajña," so too it has not been stated [in that way] here. Therefore, it is certain that the Supreme Brahman is indeed something else.

Even so, it is easy to maintain that the term *brahman* has a conventional usage among the learned (*vidvadrūḍhi*) for Viṣṇu, or a usage among those who know Brahman (*brahmavid-rūḍhi*) for Śiva; for instance, at the beginning of the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, following the six questions—"What is the cause? What is Brahman?"—the exponents of Brahman (*brahmavādinaḥ*) speak thus: [and so on].
Because of such statements as, "He who abides without distinction within all those causes, joined with Time and the Self," and "He is the Lord, the one Rudra,
Śiva alone," we understand from the usage and terminology of the knowers of Brahman that the terms *rudra* and *brahman* are interchangeable; and this [evidence] is powerful.
The conventional usage among those who know Brahman (*brahmavid-vadrūḍhi*) prevails over the usage among the learned (*vidvad-rūḍhi*), because they are superior.
Thus says the Smṛti: "Those whose intellects are fixed on the merit of the learned are superior; among those of perfected intellect, the speakers are superior;
and among speakers, the exponents of Brahman (*brahmavādinaḥ*) are superior. Therefore, the word *brahman* is primarily applied to Viṣṇu alone.
It is not so, because of the multiplicity of meanings, as in the case of words such as "cow" (*go*). Nor is the reason unestablished;

for while there is a primary sense in one instance, even in the case of words like "cow," which have multiple meanings, there is primacy in the sense of the animal (derived from the etymology *gacchati*, "it moves") and non-primacy in other senses such as heaven (*svarga*).

It may be so; yet there is no lack of proof, because a comprehensive enumeration of objects is untenable, and because it has been stated that a commonality (*anugata*) capable of serving as a delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is impossible. Therefore, it is established that for the proponents of Brahman, the Supreme Person, the Supreme Lord alone, is the Supreme Brahman.

But how can Śiva possess the status of being the Supreme Brahman? For the causality of the world's birth and so forth— which is well-known in the Vedānta scriptures as the defining characteristic [of Brahman]— is established as residing in Nārāyaṇa alone.
And likewise, it is heard in the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad, beginning with the words, "In the beginning, indeed, there was only Nārāyaṇa;
there was no Brahmā, no Īśāna, nor heaven, nor earth," [describing] the state prior to creation.
Because Nārāyaṇa exists; for passages such as, "From which indeed these beings are born," "In the beginning,
my dear, this was Being alone," and "The Self alone, indeed, was this in the beginning," establish Nārāyaṇa alone in a general form.

One should sacrifice with animals; for in such passages as "of the goat's omentum and fat," the syntactic unity between the general term and the specific qualification is established by the principle that "the goat [is meant] because of the wording of the mantra. This is further supported by such texts as "From Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā was born."

Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that even Brahmā and the others arise from Him alone. Although there are such passages as: "When there was darkness, neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being—Śiva alone existed; He was indeed Rudra, and he did not stand for a second [entity]; He is the Cause, the one to be meditated upon, possessing all sovereignty."
By such passages as "Śambhu, the Lord of all, endowed [with all attributes], in the midst of space," it is understood that Śiva also exists prior to creation; nevertheless,
because of scriptural statements such as "Rudra was born from Nārāyaṇa," the birth of Rudra is heard of.

For those who hold that Śambhu, Śiva, Rudra, and so forth are the ultimate cause, it is not logical that Nārāyaṇa alone should be the object of reference; nor should it be argued that Viṣṇu’s non-origination is established by the scriptural statement, "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— they are all produced."
"Though unborn, he manifests in many ways"—this is because it refers to his descent (avatāra).
And in the Gītā, there is the statement of Kṛṣṇa: "I am the source of all; from me everything [proceeds]."
When the emergence of unrighteousness occurs, then I manifest myself.
And in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "The Blessed One, whose self is Brahmā-Nārāyaṇa, created living beings;
hear from me how he did so, as in the case of the great sage."
O Great Sage, tell me how that Lord known as Brahmā-Nārāyaṇa created all beings at the beginning of the kalpa; and in the Uttara-Rāmāyaṇa it is said that the divine Nārāyaṇa,
bearing the conch, discus, and mace, was indeed the Creator.

And likewise, he is the destroyer of all beings. He whose work is Bhava, Brahmā, and Pitāmaha—the Grandfather; who is the glorious Bhava, the dweller on Kailāsa, the wielder of the discus, and the Source (Sambhava)—therefore, he is magnified by the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas.

If it is argued that Nārāyaṇa alone is the supreme Brahman to be known through the Vedāntas, because the *Nārāyaṇopaniṣad* reveals him as the cause of the world's birth and so forth, and thus he possesses the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) consisting in being the cause of the world's origin and the rest;

To this we reply: although the status of Viṣṇu as the cause of the world is established by scripture, there is no difference between us two in this matter; you are my power, without a doubt, and you are composed of me.
Everything is composed of the Self (manmaya), unmanifest, and has the Puruṣa as its essence.

I am the knower, you are the form of knowledge; I am the end, O Hari, you are the intellect. You are primordial nature (prakṛti), O best of gods, and I am the spirit (puruṣa); of this there is no doubt.
"You alone are the *māyā* of the universe; in me, I am [you] from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
Thus it is corroborated by the *Harivaṃśa*, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, and other sources.
Since the *Śvetāśvatara* passage establishing Śiva as the supreme cause demonstrates that He alone is the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe,
[it is concluded that] "one should merge the vital breath, along with the senses, into the mind at the end of the *nāda*, into the Supreme Self."

Having firmly established [the mind], one should meditate upon Īśāna, who is to be meditated upon; all this is Brahman, for from Brahman Viṣṇu and Rudra are produced at the end. He who is endowed with all sovereignty, the Lord of all, the causeless cause, is to be meditated upon.
Regarding the statement "Śambhu is the space...," following the description of the origin of the three lords (*īśvara*), it is understood that because [the text] says "without cause" (*akāraṇa*),
these three are equally the supreme cause; however, as for the actual cause—

However, by the word "to be meditated upon" (*dhyeya*), a distinction from the previous [state] is established; and because the supreme causality of Śambhu is thereby ordained, there is no succession of births for Viṣṇu.
Now, [one might object that] according to the Atharva-śruti and the Nārāyaṇa-śruti, [Viṣṇu arises] from the presence of Śiva and Nārāyaṇa respectively...

Regarding the birth of Brahmā and Rudra from the sky (the egg), how can there be a state of being produced by both, given their mutual opposition? Since no conceptual construction regarding a real entity is possible, if one attempts to establish their non-opposition through a distinction between different cosmic cycles (*kalpa*), this becomes impossible as it fails to establish the ultimate reality; thus, by entering the Advaita doctrine, [the result is] the featureless (*nirviśeṣa*).
If it is argued that this is because of the context of establishing Brahman as the supreme reality, it is not so;
for it is heard in scripture that Rudra, the agent of dissolution, arises immediately after Nārāyaṇa.
As it is said in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "Then Hari, having become Kālāgnirudra, the destroyer of all..."
For the remaining two [fires], arising from the breath, burn away sins below.
And in the Vāmana [incarnation], another [form] consisting of darkness likewise arose as the three-eyed one, holding a trident in his hand,
with matted hair, displaying a rosary of beads.
And in the Uttara Rāmāyaṇa, it is said: "The glorious Bhava, whose abode is Kailāsa, was born from anger."
In the Śiva-prakaraṇa of the Bhārata, it is said that the Lord created Brahmā, the source of the worlds, from his right limb,
and likewise Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting the worlds from his left side, and [the Rudras] from his heart.
"Likewise [regarding] Rudra... Thus [it is said].
Now, the intention is as follows: because it is understood from the Atharva Veda passage augmented by the Mahābhārata that all three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—are specifically objects of creation.
Because the origin of Rudra refers to Kālāgnirudra,

the negation "not the cause" serves to negate the causality of all three; furthermore, by the word "but" (*tu*), which establishes a distinction, Śambhu— who is distinct from that triad— is enjoined as the supreme cause.

Because the conception of Viṣṇu as the source of manifestation and the one intent on incarnation is dependent upon the Supreme Cause, it is untenable in the absence of that [Supreme Cause]. Therefore, it is improper to interpret words such as "Śiva" and others—which denote the Cause—as referring to Viṣṇu; for this is like the maxim of the "sacrificial animal" (*paśu*) and the "goat" (*chāga*). The same applies to words such as "Being" (*sat*) and "Self" (*ātman*).
For it is possible to assert that even terms such as "Nārāyaṇa" and others refer to Śiva.
As it is stated in the Kaivalyopaniṣad:
"He alone is Viṣṇu, he is Prāṇa, he is Time, he is Agni, and he is the Moon. [Also] in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:

And the Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord, is the support of all; for He is celebrated in the Vedas and the Vedāntas by the name Viṣṇu. He whose names are those of Viṣṇu is indeed "Viṣṇunāmā" (named after Viṣṇu).

Just as [the names] *dhuttūraka*, *kanakāhvaya*, *citraka*, and *vahni-saṃjñika* [refer to the same plant], so too does the statement from the *Atharva-upaniṣad* have the same meaning as the *Nārāyaṇa-upaniṣad*. (p. 13)

This should be understood as it was illustrated in the previous argument. Furthermore: He who is the devourer of all worlds, who will devour them, who incessantly creates, emits, or sustains them—for that reason he is called Maheśvara. And the formal syllogism (*prayoga*) is: Viṣṇu is the beginning of the world...

It is distinct from the cause, because it is distinct from Īśvara, like Brahmā and others. Nor can it be argued that this [distinction] shares the same logical status as the reflection (ābhāsa), because that would contradict the previously cited Śrutis and other authorities.
Therefore, the causality of the origin and so forth of the world, which constitutes the definition of Brahman, resides in the Supreme Lord.

Because Sadāśiva is eternally perfected, his status as the Supreme Brahman is unimpeded. Now, one might object: let there be no birth of Rudra from Viṣṇu; rather, his birth may be from Brahmā. And so it is stated in the *Bhāgavata*, the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*:
A boy, blue and red in hue, appeared upon the lap of the Lord; he then wept with a melodious voice and ran away, O best of the twice-born. To him who was weeping, Brahmā said, "Why do you weep?
He then replied to the Lord of Creatures, "Give me a name that transcends the body."

"O God, you are Rudra by name; do not weep, maintain your fortitude. Then that Lord gave him seven other names, as well as the stations for these eight, their wives, and their sons—the Lord [bestowed] Bhava, Śarva, and likewise Īśāna.
Likewise, O twice-born one, that Grandfather spoke to Bhīma, Ugra, and Mahādeva, Paśupati;
he then established these names and assigned them their respective abodes.
The Sun, water, earth, wind, fire, space, the initiated Brāhmaṇa,
and Soma— these are the [eight] bodies in their respective order.

In the Jābālopaniṣad it is said: "From the forehead Rudra is born; give me a name," and so he gave him a name. Now, if Rudra originates from Brahmā, does this not contradict the scriptural statement that "Rudra is born from Nārāyaṇa"? And it is not [the case that there is no contradiction].

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because of the distinction between different *kalpas*—since it must be stated that Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman and from him alone everything originates—we say: no. For even Brahmā is born from Nārāyaṇa; thus, just as in the passage "from space, wind," [it refers to] Viṣṇu himself in the form of the four-faced one.

There is no contradiction because [the text] is intent upon the origin of Rudra. And it is stated in the *Uttara Rāmāyaṇa* in the words of Brahmā: "Having previously condensed the worlds by means of your own *māyā*, you indeed gave birth to me while lying alone upon the single ocean."
Even as you were being born from my navel, resembling a divine lotus and the sun, the entire work pertaining to Prajāpati was entrusted by you to me.
And it is said: "The Reality is the primordial creator of the three worlds, the self-effulgent Lord.
Therefore, since Brahmā was born from the navel-lotus of Nārāyaṇa, the supreme cause, and since Rudra originated from him [Brahmā], how can he [Rudra] possess the status of the Supreme Brahman?
When the prima facie argument has been presented at length, we reply.
All this is only tenable if the four-faced one (Brahmā) were born from Nārāyaṇa;

however, that is not the case, because he was born from Rudra himself. And so it is stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "He who is the source and origin of the gods, the great seer Rudra, who transcends the universe."
"He generated Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning; may he endow us with auspicious wisdom. (Taittirīyaka). "He who is the first among the gods, the great seer who transcends all"—(Taittirīyaka).
Behold Hiraṇyagarbha being born; may the God unite us with auspiciousness.
"Because there is nothing whatsoever higher than that," and so forth.

If it is objected: "Is it not heard in scripture that the four-faced Brahmā was born from the navel-lotus of Nārāyaṇa? How then is this [account of his origin] consistent?"—it is not so; for the meaning is that Brahmā, having been produced from Rudra, entered the body of Nārāyaṇa and emerged through the path of the navel. Thus, [he is called] Nārāyaṇa.

Because it is intended as praise. Thus, in the Uttara-rāmāyaṇa, there is a statement by Rāma: "While Viṣṇu was thus asleep, Brahmā then entered his belly; and knowing him to be one of great learning, the Great Yogin entered him."
From the navel of Viṣṇu arose a lotus adorned with gold;
from that indeed emerged Brahmā, the great lord,
desiring to create the earth, the wind, the mountains, and the trees.
And again:
having seen [him], he was released by the Self-Existent One (Asvayambhū), and likewise Rātra was gazed upon.

"By that sound, Hara indeed arrived together with Hari; then, by the blow of the discus, Madhu and Kaiṭabha were slain. In this [passage], regarding the entry into and exit from Viṣṇu’s body, it was for the sake of protecting Brahmā.

Nor is it appropriate to regard [the passage] as a mere *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) on the grounds that it is intended as a eulogy— such as "You indeed gave birth to Rudra together with Viṣṇu in the beginning"— because it occurs within a context of instruction on *dharma* and because it explicitly mentions the commission of a transgression (*pratyavāya*). Regarding this, there is the statement of Jaimini in the *Vedapādastava*:
I bow to that Mahādeva, by whose command the Lord Creator fashioned this world at the beginning of the kalpa,
just as it was before.
I bow with devotion to that supreme Hara, the controller of the gods, since Nārāyaṇa stands pervading the entire world as the one to be known.

And thus, even the birth of Rudra from Brahmā is essentially an incarnation, because it takes the form of a manifestation resulting from the granting of a boon by the Supreme Lord, who was pleased by ascetic penance, in order to fulfill the request of the Four-faced One. Likewise, [the case of] Āditya...
In the twenty-fifth chapter of the Purāṇa, the speech of the Four-faced One (Brahmā) is as follows:
"I desire you alone as my son, or a son equal to you; deluded by your *māyā*, O Śambhu, I did not know you to be the Supreme Śiva. Then Īśvara said:
"O Grandfather, a son shall be born to you as a portion of myself; O sinless one, knowledge concerning me will soon arise within you."
Thus, O sinless one, by my command, that lord of yogis, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, shall become your helper; he is indeed a portion of myself, of this there is no doubt.

Therefore, since the birth of Caturmukha from Rudra is understood from the two scriptural passages of the Śvetāśvatara and Taittirīyaka Upaniṣads, those Purāṇas that contradict this by propounding his origin from the navel of Nārāyaṇa fall under the Adhikaraṇa on Apparent Contradiction (Virodhādhikaraṇa).

Because [the Purāṇas] cannot be sublated by logical reasoning (nyāya), because the statements of the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad have been established as referring to an intermediate creation, and because the emergence of the four-faced Brahmā from Nārāyaṇa is understood from the Nārāyaṇa and Kūrma Purāṇas, etc., as being of the nature of an entrance and an exit.
And because it is in the form of a hymn of praise (p.
and because Rudra’s birth from the forehead of Brahmā was brought about by the granting of a boon.

Because it is of the nature of a manifestation; for [the statement] "Rudra was born from the forehead" is like a perception of independent origination, whereas in the statements of the Atharva and the Mahābhārata there is no hearing of independent origination. On the contrary, because he is perceived as an object of creation, his dependence is understood. This is the name.

Furthermore, because the four-faced Brahmā bestowed the name [Śiva] preceded by the command of Rudra, saying, "Make him mine," and because it is established that he is distinct from the Supreme Lord, the ultimate cause, due to his being Kālāgnirudra.
"Thus meditating, from the aperture of his nose, O sinless one, he [Nārāyaṇa] suddenly emerged even from the boar-form,
having the size of a human thumb"— from this statement in the *Bhāgavata*,
the birth of Nārāyaṇa from the nose of the Four-faced One (Brahmā) is heard. In the *Vāmana Purāṇa*:
"I have no mother, nor father; likewise, I am without support and dwell upon the mountain.
O King of Mountains, I accept your daughter, given by you according to dharma, for the sake of my own delight. Thus he spoke.

Furthermore, the birth of Rudra does not proceed from the four-faced Brahmā, but rather from the word of Īśvara. For this very reason, the argument that "Rudra is not the Supreme Brahman because he is created by Nārāyaṇa, just like ourselves," is refuted.
This also applies to the inference regarding Śiva’s nature as the Supreme Reality, even in the case of Rudra.

Because the object, fire, being of the nature of a deity, lacks the status of the Supreme Brahman, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) regarding that part [of the argument]. Furthermore, due to the *Gītā* statement, "I create myself," there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) within the self itself, as it is something created by itself. Nor does the word "self" (*ātman*) refer to the body.

Since souls are also eternal, it is the body alone that is created; nor is [the soul] clearly something created, because it is the same even in its own case. Furthermore, the first part of the reason [in the syllogism] would be redundant, as such a counter-argument could be applied in every instance. Thus, the origination and so forth belong to the entire manifestation consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
It is established that Brahman is the cause, the progenitor of Viṣṇu and the other gods, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord, the bearer of Gaṅgā, and superior to all.

Now, how is it that Maheśvara, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, possesses supreme lordship over all? Since the Gaṅgā originates from the foot of Viṣṇu, and her bearing by him constitutes the bearing of the water from Viṣṇu’s foot, this serves as proof of Viṣṇu’s superiority. To explain further:
And in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa: "By the sacred water (tīrtha) of the most excellent river issuing from whose feet being held upon his head, Śiva became auspicious;
one should long meditate on that thunderbolt discharged from the mountain-like mind of the Creator."
The lotus-foot of the Blessed One.

"Regarding the phrase *tatpādasalilaṃ yathā* (just as that water from His feet): first is the water from the pitcher used for the ritual service of the Primordial Grandfather (Brahmā), and thereafter is the purifying water from the feet of the Blessed One who reclines upon the serpent."
Furthermore, in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, introducing the Gaṅgā:
"Thereafter, O Brahmin, flows that river which removes all sins, the Gaṅgā,
tawny with the unguents from the limbs of the celestial nymphs."
Having issued from the foot of Viṣṇu and having flooded the lunar orb,
Gaṅgā indeed falls from the sky all around the city of Brahmā.
Shiva bears with devotion upon his head day and night that [nectar] which has issued forth from the stream of the nail of the big toe of Viṣṇu’s left lotus-foot.

Other statements regarding this matter are also to be seen here. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Śiva is not superior to Viṣṇu, just like a disciple who carries the water from the feet of his guru.
Nor is the reason (*hetu*) non-probative, because carrying the water from the feet is performed out of devotion.
Because it does not indicate inferiority.

To this it is replied: although the Gaṅgā originates from the foot of Viṣṇu, its bearing [by devotees] does not result in degradation, because it is caused by his desire to show favor to his own devotees.

Because he holds Lakṣmī—the daughter of the great ocean of milk—constantly upon his chest, Nārāyaṇa is called Lakṣmīdhara; yet, compared to the ocean or even compared to Lakṣmī herself, he is inferior. However, there is a measure of superiority [in his case].
It is indeed even greater than their actual existence. Thus it is said in the Bālakāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa:
"O Rāma, when that God of gods had departed, he remained fasting for a year, pressing the earth down with his big toe."
Then, when a year had passed, Umāpati Paśupati, who is honored by all the worlds,
spoke thus to the king:
I am pleased with you, O best of men; I shall do what is pleasing to you. I shall bear the daughter of the king of mountains upon my head.
By such statements as these, it is shown that even when the Supreme Lord, the Blessed One, the Supreme Brahman, who is supremely compassionate and pleased by Bhagīratha’s austerity,
bore the Gaṅgā upon his head for the sake of favoring Bhagīratha, there was neither increase nor decrease [in his nature].
Moreover, the superiority of Śiva is heard in that very same place:
"O King, the earth will not be able to withstand the falling of the Gaṅgā;
indeed, O hero, we see no one other than the wielder of the trident [Śiva] capable of supporting her."
In that very place, there is a statement by Brahmā:
"Protect all these worlds; you ought not to destroy them. Having heard the words of the gods, the Great Lord of all the worlds said to them all, "So be it."
And he spoke this to Yuna.
Moreover, he is honored by the entire world as Paśupati; and there is a Vedic scripture: "To whom [is] the head bowed in salutation; to him, to him, [be] what is offered. (p.
Indeed, animals are of these two kinds: those with two feet and those with four feet. Therefore, Rudra is the lord of animals. Also, in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Sureśa (Indra), and the others are proclaimed to be animals; of them..."
Having fallen [from that state], Śiva, the Lord of beings, is remembered as Paśupati.
And that he is honored by all the worlds is stated in the *Atharvopaniṣad*:
"He who shall consume all the worlds, having consumed them, and who incessantly creates and emits them—he is called Maheśvara. Therefore...

"One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. Seeing that those two were endowed with intelligence and firmly established in the Vedas, the Lord had them taught [the Itihāsas and Purāṇas] for the purpose of augmenting the Veda. Thus [it is said].

Because the *Rāmāyaṇa* serves to supplement the Veda; for those words such as "Paśupati," which are established in the *Rāmāyaṇa* passages cited here, are honored by all the world and refer exclusively to Rudra,
they serve the purpose of supplementing the respective meanings of those terms as established in the Veda.

Because it is being recognized [as the same], and because it would contradict the respective introductory passages and so forth, it is not appropriate to interpret it as referring to another deity. Furthermore, it has been stated that the extraordinary purity of the Gaṅgā is dependent upon its connection with Maheśvara. In that very same [text]:
O dear one, those very Gandharvas who dwell upon the surface of the earth touched that water which had fallen from your body,
thinking it to be pure.
And in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "O Śambhu, she who emerged from the mass of your matted locks after flooding the gravel of bones, led the sinful sons of Sagara to heaven."
In reality, however, the Gaṅgā did not originate from the foot of Viṣṇu, but rather was produced from the Himavat.
Thus, in the Rāmāyaṇa, there is a statement by Rāma:
"Of the daughter of the King of Mountains, the eldest, in her great splendor..."
(21) By what cause does Pārvatī purify the three paths? O knower of dharma, how is Gaṅgā,
the best of rivers, renowned as the one who flows through the three paths in the three worlds?
Those who are endowed with such actions.

While the descendant of Kakutstha was speaking thus, Viśvāmitra, whose wealth is asceticism, [spoke]. Furthermore, in the section concerning the desire to know the truth, there is the speech of Brahmā:
"This Gaṅgā, the eldest daughter of Himavat, is born of the Himalayas. And the speech of Vainateya:
In that very place—
O bull among men, the Gaṅgā is the eldest daughter of Himavat;
O mighty-armed one, perform the water-libation rites for your ancestors there.

If it is argued that the Gaṅgā’s origin from Viṣṇu’s feet is established by statements in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, the *Bhāgavata*, and other texts, we say no; for by the expression "Viṣṇu’s feet," what is intended is simply the world situated above the realm of Dhruva. And so it is stated in that very same context:
The preceding statement:
"In whatever measure of space Maitreya remains fixed, the earth shall endure with patience until the dissolution of all beings."
Above and beyond the Ṛṣis, where Dhruva is established, is this divine third station of Viṣṇu, radiant in the sky.
Where merit and demerit have ceased and all causes of suffering are exhausted, having gone there they do not grieve— that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

By such statements as these— since this section is devoted to establishing the worlds beginning with Bhūta— one has described the world above Dhruva through those two specific statements, and subsequently, by means of other statements as well, established that very same world as being the "foot of Viṣṇu."
(As stated on p. 22:
"Established in this [space], the radiant one, the Pole Star (Dhruva), is himself invoked here.
O twice-born one, all luminaries are established in Dhruva; Śambhu is the light of lights. By such passages, it is that very [reality] which [is meant].

Having stated that the world known as Viṣṇupada is the support of all, and having established its very nature with the words, "Thus is this third step of Viṣṇu, consisting of pure essence," [the text continues]: "O Brahmin, from that world flows forth the river that removes all sins."

Based on the previously cited statements such as "of the limbs of the goddess Gaṅgā," and by considering both what precedes and follows the description of Gaṅgā’s emergence, the term *viṣṇupada* does not refer to a part of the body; rather, it refers to the sky (*viyat*), for *viṣṇupada* is [also] used in the masculine sense of "space" (*ākāśa*).

The term *vihāyasī* and so forth refers to the sky (*ākāśa*) as established in the *Naighaṇṭuka*. Regarding the expression *viṣṇoḥ padam*, the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*)—namely "the station of Viṣṇu"—is stronger than the etymological derivation (*yoga*), because that conventional usage is more powerful.

And the strength of that convention is seen, for example, in the case of the injunction "A chariot-maker should establish the sacred fire," where the term refers to the person by convention rather than to one who merely "makes a chariot."

Following the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that—on account of the etymological derivation as "chariot-maker" (*rathakāra*), the possibility of knowledge produced by study exists within their entitlement to study; and because, if the term were taken as referring to caste (*jāti*), there would be the burden of postulating the application of Vedic knowledge [to them]—it is concluded that it refers only to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). Subsequently, the [author] addresses the [view that] the etymological sense (*yoga*)...

Because it depends upon the power of etymological derivation (*yogavṛtti*), its cognition is delayed; whereas conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), being independent of that, is more powerful due to its rapid presentation. Therefore, only one belonging to the *rathakāra* caste is entitled to perform the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*). And by the force of that [conventional usage], the application of Vedic study (*vidyā*) must also be inferred for him.

Because it is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Nor is there any contradiction with the statement, "flowing forth from the stream of the nail of the big toe of the left lotus-foot" (p. 23), for by virtue of the context, [it refers to] the Gaṅgā.

Because there is no contradiction with numerous statements establishing the origin [of the Gaṅgā] from the Himavat, the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is possible as praise, in that the sky itself is described as her beautiful lotus-feet and the Gaṅgā as having emerged from its big toe. And such [fanciful descriptions] are observed even in the case of insentient things.
The purpose of these [passages] is praise by way of describing the constituent parts of the ritual objects as sentient beings, as in:

"The pressing-stones are the arms, the two pressing-boards are the jaws, the skin is the tongue, the pressing-stones are the teeth, the Āhavanīya fire is the mouth, and the Uttaravedi is the nose," and so forth; and this is so even when there is a contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The status of being a figurative description (*guṇavāda*) has been stated by the Bhaṭṭācāryas: "In case of contradiction, it would be a figurative description; it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) when [the fact] is already established. It is not appropriate for the statement in the *Rāmāyaṇa* which establishes that Gaṅgā is the daughter of Himavat to be considered a mere eulogy (*arthavāda*). Not so.
For it is heard right there that a boon had been granted by Brahmā, saying, "Some [being] shall be born who will speak untruthful poetry. Alternatively,
[it may be reached] through the opening of the shell of the cosmic egg, which was pierced by the nail of the big toe of Viṣṇu's foot.

The designation of [the river] as originating from the big toe is due to its entry into the interior [of the earth] by means of the flow of external waters, [thereby being called] "Kuṭilā" (the Crooked). And so it is said in the Vāmana Purāṇa:
"When the shell of the cosmic egg was split by Viṣṇu’s foot spreading from the sky, his..."

"From the tip of his foot, she [the Gaṅgā] then flowed crookedly away. Nor should it be said that she is the very same Gaṅgā, because in that same Purāṇa, the origin of the Gaṅgā is described separately.
Thus cursed by Brahmā, O Sage, the daughter of Himavat, who was composed of water, flooded the world of Brahmā as a yoginī.
Furthermore, there is no connection between Gaṅgā and the foot of Viṣṇu, as she is renowned in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Mahābhārata*, and the *Vāmana Purāṇa* as the daughter of Himavat.

It is logical that it possesses the status of "water from his feet" merely through its connection with the water of the cauldron; for otherwise, by virtue of contact with the water of a street, it would follow that it would possess the status of "street water."

Now, it might be argued that since the Gaṅgā was first produced from the foot of Viṣṇu and only later descended upon the Himavat, her status as the daughter of Himavat— having subsequently reached the earth— is merely secondary (gauṇa), just as her status as the daughter of Jahnu [is secondary]. For Himavat, too, is like Jahnu.

If it is argued that this is because she was obtained by the power of the path, it is not so; for she was first born from Menakā to Himavat and subsequently led to the heavenly world by the gods for the sake of a divine mission, and only later reached the earthly realm through the grace of Bhagīratha.
Because it is established by many authorities; and so it is said in the Rāmāyaṇa:
"Urged by the words of Rāma, the great sage Viśvāmitra began to recount the origin and birth of the Gaṅgā."
O Rāma, there is a great mountain-king named Himavat, a vast mine of minerals; he has two daughters whose beauty is peerless on earth.
Their mother was the slender-waisted one named Meruduhitā; she was known by the name Manoramā, the beloved wife of Himavat.
Then all the gods, desiring to accomplish the purpose of the deities, chose the eldest daughter of the lord of mountains as the river Gaṅgā who flows through the three paths.
Out of a desire for the welfare of the three worlds, Himavat gave his daughter Gaṅgā— who purifies the world and flows according to her own will— to Dadau according to dharma.
Having accepted [the request] for the sake of the three worlds, he who acts for the welfare of the three worlds took the Gaṅgā and departed with a heart that had achieved its purpose.
And there was another daughter of Śaila, O descendant of Raghu,
who, being rich in asceticism, performed severe penance while established in a strict vow.
The best of mountains gave his daughter Umā, who was endowed with fierce asceticism and honored by the world, to Rudra, her worthy match.
O Raghava, these two daughters of the king of mountains, honored by the worlds— the Ganga, the best of rivers, and the goddess Uma— are yours.
All this has been told to you, O dear one, best among those who go their way, regarding how the river that flows through the three paths first went to the sky.
"Thus this daughter of the lord of mountains, beautiful as the celestial river, free from sin and carrying its waters, ascended to the world of the gods. Thus [it is said].

If it is argued that, since [the Ganges] originates from the feet of Viṣṇu, the purpose of reaching the world of the gods from this world would be redundant— and even if that were so, it is established in many Purāṇas— the answer is that the perception of its origin is figurative. If one asks what the decisive factor (vinigamaka) here is, it is the color of the mother suitable for conceiving a fetus.

Because it indicates [her] first birth; for this very reason, it is stated in the *Dharmaśāstra* that being born from one's own body (*ātmajatva*) is primary in the case of the *aurasa* son, while it is secondary in the case of the *dattaka*, *krīta*, and others.
Therefore, she was not born from the feet of Viṣṇu on the Gaṅgā, because she was the daughter of Himavat, like Gaurī. Nor is it the case that...
Success; for that success was achieved through the birth from the womb of Menakā.
"Ganga, who flows from the foot of Vishnu, is borne upon the head of Shiva"— such are the Puranic statements found by the hundreds in the context of praising various deities.
(26) Desiring to know, the son of Agādha spoke again to Raghu’s bull among men: "Menā herself, the daughter of Himavat, was carried by the gods back to her own world."
And Viṣṇu, carrying on his head the water from the feet of the brahmins hundreds of times—let Śambhu be considered thus: "Is there any deficiency in me compared to them?"

Thus it is said in the *Bhāgavata*: "He, the Lord of the virtuous, who is indeed the greatest teacher of the world, bore his feet upon his head and his water upon his head while he himself was performing the service of massaging them; then, having seated him upon a couch, he joyfully fanned him."
Having brought water and washed his feet, the king, whose lineage was purified by his feet, took hold of the feet of the Blessed One, the sanctifier of the world, with his head.
Nor is there a lack of authoritative evidence for Śambhu’s superiority over Viṣṇu;
for it is said in that very same [text]:
"Neither I, nor sacrifice, nor you others, nor the sages who partake in this [world], know the truth."
Who would dare to challenge the wind, which is independent and whose measure is known by its power and vigor?

Therefore, since the Supreme Lord is understood through the descriptions of His being the highest of all and superior to the universe— qualities such as being saluted by all the worlds as stated in the Śrutis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas—
and since Gaṅgā is understood to be the daughter of Himavat, [the merit] of bearing her...

Furthermore, because he was moved by grace toward Bhagīratha, the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), the Sovereign of All, is supremely compassionate. And thus is the formal argument (*prayoga*): Śiva is devoid of any equal or superior, because he is worthy of homage from all, and because he is the Lord of all.

"That which is not thus is not thus, like us and others"— by means of this purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekyanumāna*), the superiority of Viśva is established. Nor is the reason (*hetu*) irrelevant,
because in the case of kings and others, the state of being worthy of salutation is invariably preceded by such superiority.
For the state of being worthy of universal homage is untenable without supreme preeminence;
furthermore, this would contradict the aforementioned scriptural passages and so forth— enough of this prolixity.
But surely, the supremacy of Śiva has been established by the authority of the *Rāmāyaṇa*. How, then, is that consistent? For in the *Rāmāyaṇa* itself it is said:
"Seeing that bow of Śiva strung by the prowess of Viṣṇu..."
The gods, along with the hosts of sages, likewise regarded Viṣṇu as superior.
And in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Assuming a human body, Śauri performed great deeds;
by his mere yawn, Govinda conquered Indra and all the gods with ease."
He caused Śaṅkara to yawn; overcome by the yawn, Hara sat down on the seat of the chariot and was unable to fight with Kṛṣṇa, whose deeds are effortless.

If it is argued that even elsewhere—in the *Bhāgavata*, the *Harivaṃśa*, and so forth—a defeat caused by Bāṇāsura is heard of [Viṣṇu], how then can there be the superiority of Śiva? Do not say so. Is the superiority of Viṣṇu asserted on the basis of the statements in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, or [on the basis of] the *Rāmāyaṇa*?

Or [is it] from a direct statement? Not the first, because in that very context, the removal of the itching of the arms resulting from the severing of the arms of the demon Bāṇa was in accordance with the command of Īśvara.
And so it is heard in that very place:
Then Bāṇa, having prostrated before the three-eyed god, said: "O Lord, I am weary of these thousand arms without a battle."
Perhaps one among these arms of mine will become the cause of their success without a battle; otherwise, what is the use of my arms as a mere burden?
Śaṅkara said:
"O Bāṇa, when the destruction of your peacock-banner occurs,
you shall then attain that joy which delights all people."
(28) Thus, the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Brahman, who is supremely compassionate,
bestowed grace upon Bāṇāsura, [removing] his defects such as egoism and the like.

Since it is improper for one to personally remove that [suffering]— according to the maxim that even a poisonous tree, having been nurtured, cannot be fit to be cut down by its own grower— one intends to remove it through another means, which results in the ultimate favor toward him.
With the words, "O you whose banner is the peacock, you have granted me this boon— the form of battle that allays the itching of my arms," and so forth, he [Śiva] bestowed it;
for a battle with Bāṇa was not possible without the yawning of Śaṅkara.

Nor was the status of gatekeeper of his own city previously desired by the Supreme Lord, who was pleased by the ascetic penance of Bāṇāsura, for the sake of warding off fear from Indra and the other gods; therefore, [the Lord granted] Bāṇa’s desired [position].
It is proper that the Supreme Lord, having made a promise, should not engage in battle while standing at the gate; therefore, it was by Viśvarāja alone, acting under the authority of another,
that Bāṇa was instructed by Kṛṣṇa for the sake of fulfilling the boon granted by the Lord.
There is no loss of superiority for the Lord. Otherwise—[it would have been said]:
"Even though he is arrogant due to this [boon], he is not to be slain by you; since this Daitya has been granted a boon by me, I therefore beg your forgiveness."
Thus, there would be no compliance with the command of the Lord;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the need for] a counter-measure against the restraint of Brahmā and Kāma. If it is argued that this is a hymn of praise for Kṛṣṇa, [we reply that] great-souled ones are free from envy.

It is well known everywhere that [the gods] accomplish their own purposes by praising and fondling disciples and others who carry out their commands; this entire narrative, ending with the marriage of Uṣā and Aniruddha, was likewise [accomplished] by the Supreme Lord.
(29) "It was intended" means that it was previously given as a dowry by Pārvatī, who understood his intention. And so it is said in that very Purāṇa:
"On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, he who shall overcome you in a dream will become your husband; you shall become a princess.
On the contrary, in the Vāmana Purāṇa, following Rudra’s departure after the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice:
Since even equality is difficult to attain by hearing of Viṣṇu’s flight,
how much more so superiority?
Seeing the matted-haired one with eyes bloodshot from anger, Hari moved away from that place; Kubja, however, remained there, hidden from view.

Therefore, the *Rāmāyaṇa* passage beginning with "They considered Viṣṇu to be superior" should be understood as explained above; for the mere cognition of superiority, being common to both valid knowledge (*pramā*) and error (*bhrama*), does not establish actual superiority. Nor [is this the case] for the gods...
It is appropriate that he possesses knowledge of reality (*tattvajñatva*), because he is presented as one who desires to know the supreme excellence (*ādhikya*) in that very context.

In the section concerning the destruction of Tripura, it is heard in scripture that Sadāśiva’s superiority over Nārāyaṇa is due to his superior knowledge, while Nārāyaṇa’s subordination to him is due to being impelled by him.

They said, "Rudra. Rudra is indeed fierce (*krūra*). Since there were three cities of those Asuras here, and because Viṣṇu was established as the arrow as an instrument for the task of conquering Tripura, Rudra is independent by virtue of being the one who employs that [arrow].

Because the understanding of [Viṣṇu’s] agency makes his superiority manifest, it is logical that the knowledge of superiority expressed in such statements as "they considered Viṣṇu superior" is indeed an error;
otherwise, [if it were not an error], he would have been capable of breaking even Mount Meru with that bow.
p.
30) For the sake of Viṣṇu’s capable son Rāma’s victory over Rāvaṇa and others, and for the destruction of Trikūṭa, which served as Rāvaṇa’s abode and was a part of Mount Meru.
There would be no experience of great exertion for him. However, when Rāvaṇa lifted up Kailāsa, Śiva merely moved his big toe to subdue him;
he did not experience great exertion as Rāma did. Thus, his superiority is evident. Likewise:
And there is the statement of Abhiyukta:
"The earth, having slipped from the head of the lazy one whose big toe had entered Pātāla, surely fell upon you; thus, when he has grown fat, the wicked man becomes deluded."
And this matter is to be seen in the *Uttararāmāyaṇa*: "Then Mahādeva,
laughing at what he had done, playfully pressed that mountain with his big toe."
Then, their arms being thus oppressed by Rāvaṇa,
the ministers of that Rākṣasa were struck with amazement;
for a truly great cry was let out by that chief of Rākṣasas as his arms were crushed by the mountain.
By whom the three worlds were filled.

Therefore, because the statement spoken by Paraśurāma— who was a partial incarnation of Viṣṇu— for the sake of self-glorification was rooted in egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), they considered Viṣṇu to be superior; this is the reason,
just as in the case of the sentence "the Adhvaryu priest takes the garment used for the *vaisarjana* offering," which is rooted in greed (*lobha*).
By the principle of the section on perception (*darśanādhikaraṇa*), lack of authority is inevitable; therefore, enough with this excessive detail.

Is it not well known in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas that in the conquest of Tripura, Mount Meru was the bow-bearer and chariot of the Supreme Lord, the moon and sun were the two wheels, the Vedas were the horses, the four-faced Brahmā was the charioteer, and Nārāyaṇa was the arrow?

31) Although its superiority [is established] by virtue of being the instrument for Brahmā and the others, nevertheless, that should be understood from the very section on the conquest of Tripura cited previously. Furthermore, there is the request for the boon of Pāśupata [status].

How is this justified? If it is argued that begging is rooted in wretchedness and is therefore contrary to excellence, it is said in reply: although the state of being a Pāśupata is established as beginningless, the compassionate Lord Parameśvara [bestowed] the knowledge of Pāśupata...

Intending to accomplish the supreme goal of human existence and desiring to favor the gods— who were devoid of that knowledge— by instructing them, he brought them face-to-face under the pretext of demonstrating the benefit of conquering the cities, and then taught them the Pāśupata [discipline].

He said, "I choose this boon: 'May I alone be the lord of animals,'" by these words. If it is asked, "But since the request 'choose a boon' is understood, how is that [statement] appropriate?"—do not say so; for [it implies] his own supremacy over the gods.

We say that [the purpose] is to cause [them] to accept it precisely through his mouth. And it is appropriate that the Supreme Lord, who is omniscient, acts as a teacher toward his sons out of great respect for them, just like a father; for the status of being a father to the gods is also heard in the Rudra-sūkta.

"—let the favor of the Maruts come to us. Nor is the established status of the Pāśupatas and others unproven; for cattle indeed belong to Prajāpati, and Rudra is their overlord. Furthermore, it is not logical that he (Rudra) should be considered adventitious, as the Veda is eternal.

Because it would entail the fault known as "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*). For it is not logical that the beginningless Veda should be the proponent of the Pāśupata system, which has a beginning. If it is argued that passages such as "Hariścandra, indeed, was a king" might be beginningless, [we reply: they...

For the quality of being beginningless in the form of a continuous stream has been demonstrated in the *Arthavāda* section of the *Śābarabhāṣya* on the *Jaiminisūtra*, for the purpose of avoiding the objection regarding connection with the non-eternal.

Nor is it logical that Rudra’s status as a Pāśupata (or subordinate to Paśupati) should also be so; for from Vedic passages such as the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, which state, "Rudra is one alone, there is no second," and so forth,
Rudra's oneness is understood, and thus it is possible for the Supreme Lord to be beginningless by his very nature.

Because it is untenable for [the world] to be beginningless in the form of a continuous stream; however, there is no contradiction in such passages as "those Rudras by the thousands upon thousands who exist in the world," because they are Rudras who are incarnations of the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, this [text] describes the supreme lordship of the Supreme Lord.
The Vaiṣṇava disputant, asserting that [the Puṣpaka chariot] was obtained as a boon, is outside the Vedic fold. Not the first [position], for even he [must acknowledge]:
"Having received a boon from the deities and having raised the monkeys up, Rāma, surrounded by his friends, set out for Ayodhyā by means of the Puṣpaka," according to the Rāmāyaṇa.

Because the statement is authoritative, even Viṣṇu would be subject to inferiority due to his being engaged in the act of requesting boons. And in the Śruti it is said: "What indeed is that intermediate entity by which these two are held apart? Both are held apart by Viṣṇu."
Regarding the word "bhūmi," following the question and answer, [it is explained] by such passages as: "What do they call the strength of Viṣṇu?
What is his splendor? What is his supreme resort? That one God who supported both the trembling worlds (rodasī)?
and so forth; thus, the strength, splendor, and supreme resort of Viṣṇu, as well as heaven and earth, [are described].

Regarding the question of whether the efficacy of the *dhāraṇās* is employed through their own power or through the power of another, the answers to those questions heard in that very context establish that they are employed by another.
"They say that from the wind (vāta) comes the strength of Viṣṇu; from the imperishable (akṣara), radiance is said to arise.

From the three steps (tripada), the Lord sustained that which is the single, supreme [step] of Viṣṇu. The fires and the winds—this is his ultimate resort. By such passages, [the sequence of] wind, the imperishable, the three steps, and fire [is established].
(On page 33:

There would be a depreciation [of the teaching] because it is established that Viṣṇu’s power and so forth are employed by those things denoted by the words "wind" and so on; nor, in this case, is there anything denoted by the word "Viṣṇu."

No one other than Nārāyaṇa can be [the creator], because it is impossible for anyone else to sustain heaven and earth; furthermore, it is heard in scripture that even the greatness of Viṣṇu is dependent upon his actions:
"Viṣṇu indeed desired, 'May I hear a verse of praise, but not myself.'"

Because it is established that for Viṣṇu, whose name is to be heard and celebrated as meritorious, fame is the primary motive; not the second [alternative], because for you, who deny the authority of the Vedas,
the state of being a Pāśupata as taught by the Vedas [is untenable].

Because the faults based on the *varaṇa* (choice/acceptance) are themselves seized by the fault of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). In reality, however, the *varaṇa* of Pāśupata merely establishes superiority; it does not bring about inferiority, just like the request made by Viṣṇu to Madhu and Kaiṭabha. Thus:
And in the Mārkaṇፍeya Purāṇa:
"Those two, intoxicated by excessive strength and deluded by Mahāmāyā, said to Keśava: 'Choose a boon from us.'"
The Blessed One said:
"Since both of you are to be slain by me today, I am pleased with you; what need is there for any other boon?
For this much alone has been requested by me."
And in the present context, since the solicitation of boons from the deities results in the attainment of one's own preeminence—

just as, even for a prince consecrated in a universal empire by ministers, priests, vassals, and others, his status as sovereign, his authority, and his independence are determined by the deities— so it is here.

Even the establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*) in the *Pāśupata* [tradition] results in the state of being the owner (*svāmitva*) of that Supreme Lord, as it culminates in His ownership in relation to that [establishment]. Furthermore, since there is a contradiction if those [scriptures] were to be self-validating (*svanigamya*), there is a superiority [of the Pāśupata tradition], just like a husband who has chosen his bride himself when she was sought by others.
Because He is the ultimate goal, Śiva is superior to all, as He is the Lord of all;
otherwise, like the individual soul (jīva). All others besides Śiva are governed by Śiva, because they possess the nature of bound souls (paśu).

Like ourselves and others. The quality of being the sole controller of all resides exclusively in Śiva, because it is a functional attribute that exists nowhere else other than in Śiva, just like the nature of Śiva himself. Nor is this argument unproven, as it would contradict the previously cited scriptures that establish the state of being the Lord of Paśus (Pāśupatya). Let this suffice.

Now, as for how it is stated that supremacy does not exist in anyone other than Śiva— that being impossible because supremacy belongs to Viṣṇu alone— we clearly perceive the presence or absence of supremacy through the relationship of the worshipped and the worshipper. And so it is said in the Padmapurāṇa:
The Supreme Lord said:
O Pārvatī, as I hear names beginning with the letter 'Ra', my mind attains clarity through the suspicion that they might be the name "Rāma."
And elsewhere:
"To you who are about to die, dwelling halfway in the water within the pericarp of the jewel,
I impart the mantra known as the Tāraka Brahman."
"O Śrī Rāma, 'Rāma, Rāma, Rāma'—this is indeed declared to be the *tāraka* [mantra]. Therefore, you, O Lord of Jānakī, are certainly the Supreme Brahman."
Deluded by your māyā, all do not know you in reality, even though they bow to you.
And in the *Tāpanīya*: "The bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) chanted the mantra of Śrī Rāma in Kāśī;
thus, for Śiva, who is a devotee, Rāma is one born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa."

By means of both the instruction for the recitation (*japa*) of the *brahmamantra* that bestows liberation and his own state of being a devotee (*tadbhakta*), [the text] makes known that very devotion.
And thus is the formal argument (*prayoga*): Śiva is not inferior to Nārāyaṇa, because he is a devotee of Him, and because he is His worshiper.
Because he is one who recites its mantra, like Nārada and others.
35) Nor is this [reason] non-conclusive, because the relationship of being the object of meditation and the meditator involves a state of being either inferior or superior.

If it is argued that Nārāyaṇa alone is said to be superior because he is established in common worldly usage as pervading all states of being—just as a king’s servant [is subordinate] to the king—we reply to this:
that would be tenable only if the *tāraka* mantra of Rāma were indeed a designation for Viṣṇu; but it is not.
The state of being Viṣṇu is not the basis for the application [of the term]; for there is a lack of evidence for that being the case.

According to the statement in the Skanda Purāṇa, "Yogins delight in the infinite, true, blissful Self of consciousness," the Supreme Brahman is denoted by the word *rāma*; thus, regarding the word *rāma*—

Because it is understood that [the term] denotes the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*). Nor should it be argued that this statement is consistent even if Viṣṇu were the Supreme Brahman; for it is heard in scripture that one who has attained liberation by receiving the instruction on the *Rāmatāraka* mantra at Kāśī attains the state of Śiva. Thus, his...
Because it is impossible for it to denote Viṣṇu; for the Śruti states: "As a person intends in this world, so does he become after departing from here. The meaning of this is as follows:

*Kratu* means volition (*saṃkalpa*). A person in this world is of such a nature as his volition is, and he possesses such a form of worship as he has. Having departed from here and cast off the body, he becomes exactly like that; this is the meaning. There is a statement by Kṛṣṇa in the *Gītā*:
Whatever state one constantly remembers while casting off the body at the end, to that very state one goes,
O son of Kuntī, being perpetually permeated by that state.
In that city, O Śaṅkara, the courtesans were smeared with ashes, surrounded by bees,
and their bodies adorned with moon-like ornaments, just like you.
Does the word "Rāma" denote Viṣṇu, or does it denote his incarnation? Not the first, because it is not included among the synonyms for Viṣṇu in the Nighaṇṭu and other such works.
The second [alternative] is not tenable. Even if it were to apply to him, would it denote Bhārgava Rāma, or Rāghava Rāma, or Yādava Rāma, or all of them?

Not the first; for in your own view, since you do not accept the worshipfulness of Bhārgava-Rāma as being equal to the other incarnations, it would follow that even his name must be treated with disrespect. Nor the second; [for it is said]: "I shall indeed become Rāma for the sake of subduing the wicked."
In the *Harivaṃśa-śeṣadharma*, according to the words of Virūpākṣa addressed to the great sage Mataṅga,

it is stated that because Rāmabhadra is a portion (*aṃśa*) of Sadāśiva, who is the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*), he is denotable by the word "Rāma," which signifies the Supreme Brahman. Nor is he merely half of Viṣṇu.
"O highly fortunate one, [he] begot a son for Kausalyā"—thus there is a contradiction with the statement from the *Rāmāyaṇa*.

According to the principle that "the king was fashioned from the portions (*mātrā*) of the eight world-protectors," protection is the duty of Viṣṇu; therefore, it is logical that he is a portion (*aṃśa*) of Viṣṇu. He is not non-Viṣṇu.

This is according to the maxim "the lord of the earth" (pṛthivīpati). Nor is it proper to conclude from this alone that the word *rāma* denotes Viṣṇu; for Śiva alone is the primary [referent], and according to the maxim "designations are made according to what is predominant," its denotation of Śiva is established.

Nor is Viṣṇu alone the primary agent, because his incarnation was for the purpose of destroying the Rākṣasas, and destruction is the function of Rudra; as stated in the Rāmāyaṇa in the words of Rāmabhadra: "This terrible power belongs either to him [Viṣṇu], or to me, or to Tryambaka."

Just as in the expressions "the sky has the form of the sky" and "the ocean is like the ocean," where the relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*) is intended despite their non-difference, so too—
in the case of objects composed of the five elements such as a jar— it is understood that the aspect of Rudra alone is primary.

Just as there is the conventional usage of "earthenness," "luminousness," and so forth regarding objects, [so it is here] because the portion belonging to Rudra is predominant, [there is the usage] of the word "Rāma. (p. 37)

This is because it is logically established that [the name] denotes Rudra; furthermore, in the Purāṇas, Rāma is seen to be of the nature of Śiva even by his own hand, as it is said: "In fear of enemies, in fear of thieves, and likewise in fear of kings..."
Having meditated upon the Lord of the Raghus, who was enraged like another fire of universal destruction.
Wearing a yellow-black antelope skin, his body smeared with ashes, his circle of arms drawing a bow drawn back to the ear, accompanied by Jānaki and Lakṣmaṇa,
and adorned with a crown of matted locks.

This is because practices such as wearing matted hair (*jaṭā*) and smearing oneself with ashes (*bhasmoddhūlana*) indicate the distinction of Śiva. For this very reason, Rāmabhadra is [renowned] for having established numerous *liṅgas*, such as Rāmeśvara, and for being the founder of the tradition of Śiva-worship.

Furthermore, because it is established in the *Rāmāṣṭottaraśatanāmastotra* through such statements as "the installer of the Śivaliṅga is free from all defects," and because this is also propounded in the *Purāṇa-saṃhitās* such as the *Śivarāghava-saṃvāda*, [he is] by virtue of that very nature...
The state of being denotable by the word "Rāma. By this, the third and fourth positions are also refuted;
for there is no possibility of Rāma’s identity with Brahman [in those views]. Nor is the fourth [position] tenable;
because the incarnations have a beginning, if the word "Rāma" were to denote them, [it would follow that the word is non-eternal].

If the relationship between word and meaning were non-eternal, it would contradict the Jaiminiya Sūtra which states: "The relationship of a word with its meaning is innate and eternal. Nor can it be argued that because Nārāyaṇa—the source of that [Veda]—is beginningless, their relationship is also beginningless.

Because it has been stated that there is no mention [of such a name] among the synonyms denoting that [deity]; nor does the recitation of the *Viṣṇusahasranāma* establish its status as a synonym for Viṣṇu.
This is because the recitation of the *Śivasahasranāma* is logically established as denoting that very state. And thus,

for one liberated through the worship of the Rāma-mantra by attaining the nature of Śiva, there are such scriptural statements as "he reaches the world of Vaikuṇṭha along with ten ancestors and ten descendants," which apply to the worshipper of Rāma.

Furthermore, the statements in the Dakṣa Purāṇa regarding the attainment of Vaikuṇṭha are consistent with the attainment of the deities of the *arcirādi* path as a means to reaching the world of Śiva;
or else, there is no contradiction because they concern practices performed with the desire for the world of Viṣṇu. As for Rāma...

According to the *Harivaṃśa*, the *Śeṣa*, and the teachings on Dharma, Rāmabhadra is an incarnation of Sadāśiva; therefore, the word denoting him refers to Śiva. This is because his status as Śiva is determined by his role as the founder of Rāmeśvara and other shrines, and by his wearing matted hair and ashes.

Since the *rāmatāraka* mantra that denotes him expresses Brahman— which is of the nature of truth, bliss, and consciousness— and since the instruction for the recitation (*japa*) of such a Rāma-mantra is for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world, there is neither increase nor decrease in the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord.
Success!

This might be the case: if Rāma and others performed the installation of Śiva and so forth, how then can there be a prohibition against the grace (*prasāda*) of Śiva? Nor is it logical to argue that because it is prescribed [as a duty], it must be performed, while because it is prohibited, the grace and such must not be accepted.

In the absence of consuming the remnants of the oblation, just as there would be a deficiency in the sacrifice due to the absence of a purificatory rite (saṃskāra) beneficial to the spirit— as in the case of "he eats the black antelope horn"— there would likewise follow a deficiency in the worship if the consumption of the *prasāda* were absent; therefore, the *prasāda* is accepted.
In the absence of eating [the food] as a gift of grace (*prasāda*), there arises the fault of being a mere consumer and a mere eater of that which was cooked for one's own sake.

This is because its absence would entail the violation of scriptural and traditional injunctions, such as: "But those who cook for their own sake eat sin; they eat what is evil" (Śruti). Thus, it follows that this [eating as *prasāda*] must exist.
Therefore, the prohibition of Śiva’s prasāda results in the prohibition of his worship;
39) however, the prohibition of Viṣṇu’s prasāda does not apply in this way, but rather his worship is expressly enjoined.
As it is said in the Bhāgavata: "O Lord, by partaking of the garlands, perfumes, garments, and ornaments used by You,
and by receiving Your remnants as food, may we conquer Your Māyā."
And elsewhere it is said:
"The auspicious water from the feet of Viṣṇu removes untimely death, destroys all diseases, and annihilates all misfortunes."
Furthermore:
"By those who desire to perform atonement for sins committed since birth,
let the water of the Śālagrāma stone, which removes all evil, be resorted to."
Indeed, for one who partakes of the food offering (naivedya) of Śiva’s grace,
as well as my own, that man shall himself become the expiation (prāyaścitti) in this world.

If it is argued that this is because the consumption of Śiva’s prasāda is prohibited by such statements as these, we say no. Although the prohibition of Śiva’s prasāda is heard here and there, nevertheless, its acceptance must necessarily be performed because it is enjoined. Furthermore, there is no contradiction between an injunction and a prohibition.
Because a prohibition has as its scope that which is already established by natural inclination, it refers to something other than what is specifically enjoined;
for [the rule] "one shall not [eat] all beings" would not be [a valid prohibition], just like [the injunction] "one should sacrifice a beast to Agni and Soma.
And so says the Śruti:
All this, whatever moves in this world, is pervaded by the Lord; with that renounced, you should enjoy, without coveting the wealth of anyone whatsoever.
In this context, because the word *īśa* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring to Śiva— given that "Śambhu, Īśa, Paśupati" [are synonyms for him]—
