and because it is accepted that even the usage of barbarians (*mleccha*) can be a cause for determining the meaning of a word (as in the case of "one should sacrifice a cuckoo," etc.), [the term *īśvara*] refers to Śiva despite its being in the instrumental case; for [the root] *īś* signifies sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

Because it is always intent upon Śiva by virtue of having arisen from the [Śiva]dhātu; and because, as in the case of expressions such as "inā deśā bhāvasya" and "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ," there is metrical correctness even when [the forms] are not [grammatically] standard.

Since it is understood from the injunction that [the offering] is for the purpose of eating, and since the meaning of the injunction culminates in the sense that "one should accomplish the meal with the substance offered to the Supreme Lord— which has been relinquished by him as the means for the prescribed eating"— there is the use of two non-co-referential (vyadhikaraṇa) instrumental cases in the phrase "by that which was relinquished by him."
The statement "Do not covet the wealth of anyone" is a *nindārthavāda* (deprecatory explanatory passage) connected with the yoga [of renunciation], because its status as an injunction is certain—
just like the passage "Neither by ritual action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone some have attained immortality"—
and because of the rule "He performs the *upāṃśuyāja* at the end."

Because the status of being an injunction is established just as the status of being an injunction is postulated [for other texts], for if that which has been enjoined were prohibited, it would result in the destruction of the option (*vikalpa*). As stated in the *Āditya Purāṇa*:
"Whether one be a killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or a violator of the Guru’s bed—whoever, at the time of death..."
By remembering Śiva, one shall attain union with Śiva.
One who devoutly wears on one's head the floral remains (nirmālya) of the Lord of Pārvatī obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Whoever shall wear with devotion on his head the remains of the offerings to Śiva— even if he be impure,
transgressor of moral boundaries, or fallen into any state whatsoever— [shall attain the highest goal].
Whether he be self-willed, intoxicated by pride, or excluded from religious observances,
Śaṅkara indeed destroys all his sins.
Out of greed, one should not desire nor consume the *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) of Śambhu; nor should one even touch it.
Transgressing the *nirmālya* leads to a fall from one's status. The giver of *nirmālya* is cooked in hell for an inexhaustible period of time.
The great holy ford Purudaka, the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers, as well as the Narmadā,
Kāverī, and Godāvarī rivers.
O Sage, these [deities] are always present in the water from Śambhu’s feet; for that water from Śambhu’s feet is indeed composed of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
By means of this retention, one is instantly liberated from the multitude of sins.
In the case of a self-manifested (svayambhū) linga, one made of stone, one made of jewels, one fashioned from metal, or one consecrated by a perfected being (siddha),
there shall be no appointment of a Caṇḍa.

Therefore, since the use of *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) is enjoined by these statements, and since the prohibitory statements apply to non-devotees and concern matters obtained through worldly attachment (*rāga*), the matter is settled by the Vedic injunction itself; thus, service to the *nirmālya* with devotion is a means for attaining infinite fruit.
Because it has been established [thus]. In the fourth book (*skandha*) of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*:
"Do others, such as Brahmā and the rest, not constantly know that which is called Śiva, having scattered his garlands, ashes, and human skulls upon the cremation grounds frequented by *piśācas*?"
They bear upon their heads those feet with which [the Lord] has cast [them down].
In the Rāmāyaṇa:
"There, the celestial sages, Gandharvas, and those dwelling upon the surface of the earth, touched the water fallen from Bhava’s body, considering it to be pure. Thus [it is said].
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "Emerging from the mass of Śambhu’s matted locks, she [Gaṅgā], having washed away the bones and gravel,
led the sinful sons of Sagara to heaven."

Since the service of Śiva’s grace, his foot-water, and his flower-remains (nirmālya) is enjoined by the words of the Āditya-purāṇa, Bhāgavata, Rāmāyaṇa, and Viṣṇu-purāṇa, which are further augmented by the *Īśāvāsya* Upaniṣad, this must be performed by everyone. And so it is said in the Vātūlāgama:
O beloved, the water from the feet of the Destroyer of Cities is supreme for removing the snare of bondage; it is the medicine for gout, leprosy, epilepsy, and fevers.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Having drunk the water from the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) of the God of gods, one becomes pure."
One is liberated even from such sins as consumption, epilepsy, leprosy, and the like.
And thus the formal argument (*prayoga*):

Service to Śiva’s grace and so forth is a cause for the unsurpassed human goal (*puruṣārtha*), because it is enjoined by the Veda as such, like the Aśvamedha sacrifice and others. Service to grace and so forth [is not] a powerful undesirable [result].

Is it not the case that [the act] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*) because it is enjoined, like the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites? Nor is there a lack of causal efficacy (*aprayojakatva*), because since there is no prohibition regarding what is enjoined, it is not connected with a powerful undesired consequence (*balavadaniṣṭa*). If that which is enjoined were connected with a powerful undesired consequence, the Veda would be unauthoritative (*anāpta*).

There would be the undesirable consequence [of the sacrifice] being considered "excellent" (*praṇīta*). Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the reason because of the fact that the Śyena and other such sacrifices are enjoined; for it is said: "One who has practiced sorcery (*abhicāra*) removes that sorcery, even if deficient by a goat, by means of the three...
Thus, through both the prohibition and the instruction on expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the purpose of the injunction regarding the Śyena and others is established.

Because there is no state of being an initiator for that which has not already begun to function; and because one who is engaged in the killing of an enemy is merely subject to an injunction and thus intent solely upon the means [of action]. Alternatively, the qualification "not being censured" (*avigītatva*) should be supplied; this is to be inferred by the wise.
In this regard, some maintain that the Purāṇas and Āgamas that propound Śiva are characterized by *tamas*. Their intention is as follows: in the *Matsya Purāṇa*, it is stated:
"In whichever Kalpas [these] are mixed, characterized by *tamas*, or likewise *sāttvika* and *rājasa*..."
That which was proclaimed of old by Brahmā in ancient times.
The greatness of each [deity] is described according to its true nature; the greatness of Agni and Śiva is proclaimed in the Tāmasa scriptures.
They know that the majesty of Brahmā is greater in the *rājasa* [ages],
while in the *sāttvika* kalpas, the majesty of Hari is greater; in those very [kalpas], yoga...
Having attained perfection, they shall go to the supreme goal.

"In places where [the qualities] are mixed, they know the majesty of Sarasvatī to be supreme. This is what is meant: although the Lord of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is Brahman, even for him, in certain days, *sattva* is predominant; in some, *tamas*; and in others, *rajas*. Thus...

Furthermore, some kalpas are predominantly characterized by sattva, some by rajas, and some by tamas. Consequently, when there is mutual contradiction between those Purāṇas spoken by Brahmā that belong to the sattva-predominant [kalpas] and those belonging to the others, [the following applies].

The Purāṇa alone is declared to be *sāttvika* and thus authoritative; other [texts] that contradict it are not authoritative because they were spoken by a Brahmin established in *sattva* who received them from a source. And in the Gītā:
"From *sattva* arises knowledge, and from *rajas* indeed greed; negligence and delusion [arise from *tamas*]."
Through *tamas* there may arise both knowledge and ignorance, as well as engagement and withdrawal,
what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fear and fearlessness.
That intellect which understands both bondage and liberation is purposeful and characterized by sattva.
That intellect which correctly discerns what is dharma and what is adharma, as well as what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, is the royal wisdom of the Arthaśāstra.

"That intellect which, under the influence of darkness (tamas), perceives unrighteousness as righteousness and regards all objects in a perverted manner—that, O Arjuna, is the intellect characterized by tamas. Thus [it is said].
Having indeed acquired all the meanings of the Purāṇas from the presence of Brahmā, all...
The authors of the Purāṇas composed the Purāṇas; as it has been said:
"I shall relate just as it was told of old by Dakṣa and the other most excellent sages.
Being thus questioned, the Blessed One, the lotus-born Grandfather, replied.
Therefore, because they were spoken by Brahmā— who was characterized by a predominance of *sattva* and so forth— among those of a *sāttvika* nature and others,
the Purāṇas receive the designations of *sāttvika* and so on, according to the statement: "The majesty of Agni-Śiva is proclaimed in the *tāmasa* [Purāṇas]."

The Purāṇas that propound Śiva are of the nature of *tamas*, and because Śiva is their subject matter, Śiva himself is characterized by *tamas*. This is because of such statements as: "He does not lead one to the highest good (*śreyas*); through *tamas* there is only delusion," and so forth. From *sattva*, however, [right knowledge] is born.

Knowledge leads to the highest goods (*śreyas*). For it is stated in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*: "In that regard, for men who possess the body of a being (*satvatanoḥ*), [knowledge] shall indeed exist. Because knowledge is His primary attribute, Viṣṇu alone is the bestower of the highest good.
Others, however—
"In this way, I shall quickly create delusion; from this, delusion will spread for leagues. O Rudra, O mighty-armed one, you indeed must cause the delusive scriptures to be composed."
O mighty-armed one, display what is unreal as if it were real;
manifest yourself and render me invisible.
Based on such statements from the Varāha Purāṇa, some claim that those texts which establish Śiva lack authority because they have delusion as their purpose. That is incorrect;
for although it is universally established that the quality of *tamas* (darkness) is the cause of delusion, nevertheless, regarding Śiva—
Furthermore, there is no evidence to establish that the Purāṇas and Āgamas which expound that [doctrine] are characterized by *tāmasa* (darkness). To explain: what is this "being *tāmasa*"?
Is it being produced from the quality of *tamas*, or is it being produced from *tamas* unassociated with its other qualities?

Alternatively, [the definition] may be: being produced by a darkness that is not overcome by others; or being characterized by being produced by the quality of darkness (tamas); or having an agent characterized by darkness as its creator; or being a proponent of [an entity] characterized by the quality of darkness.

[Is it] being the object to be propounded by [the principle of] Tamas as the predominant quality, or something else? Not the first, because Rudra and the other selves are eternal and therefore not characterized by Tamas; and because the entire phenomenal world is produced from the three qualities (guṇas), this applies even to the Purāṇas and Āgamas accepted by you.
Because it would entail the consequence of being purely *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness). Nor is it intended that [the effect] be produced by *tamas* alone;
for it is unestablished that a single [guṇa] can be a producer, since every guṇa produces only when conjoined with another guṇa. For this very reason, the second [alternative] is not tenable;
for every guṇa is a generator only when associated with another guṇa, and thus a guṇa of *tamas* unmixed with others [cannot be a cause].

The third [alternative] is not tenable, because the state of being produced (*janyatva*) is unestablished. Nor is it the third [option], because Rudra is eternally established, and thus that [state of being produced] is unestablished in the present context. [Furthermore, it is said: "The son of Satyavatī is the author of the Śaiva Āgamas and the eighteen Purāṇas, which have him as their author."
And also by means of narratives, sub-narratives, verses, and purifications of the ritual codes.
"Being an expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas, he composed the Purāṇa-saṃhitā"—

from this statement in the Viṣṇu-purāṇa, it follows that none of the works composed by Vyāsa possess the quality of *tāmasa* (darkness). Otherwise, even those [works] favored by you would likewise be [tāmasa].

The consequence of [Rudra] being characterized by *tamas* follows, because the same logic applies. Now, let the fourth position be that Rudra—who is qualified by a body and so forth produced from the quality of *tamas*—is indeed *tāmasa*. This is because Rudra is the agent of dissolution (*saṃhāra*).
If it is argued that this is because [the act of dissolution] is well-known in all the Purāṇas as being the effect of the quality of *tamas*, we say: not so.

For if Viṣṇu were the agent of dissolution, he would incur the undesirable consequence of not being the Supreme Lord (*anīśvaratva*). Nor is it the case that Viṣṇu is the cause of dissolution only by means of the bodies of Rudra and others.
However, it must be stated that [the quality of tamas] applies directly to protection (*pālana*).
For, since the agency of direct destruction (*saṃhārakartṛtva*) is absent in fire, its possession of the quality of tamas (*tāmasatva*) is not established.

Furthermore, because you have stated that Saṅkarṣaṇa alone possesses the nature of the destroyer, and since there is no evidence for a hierarchy when causality— whether direct or indirect— is possible everywhere,
he too must be characterized as *tāmasa*.

Because it would lead to an absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*), and because the opposite could equally be asserted; for since protection is brought about by the quality of goodness (*sattva-guṇa*) belonging to primordial nature (*prakṛti*), it would follow as a consequence that Viṣṇu himself is of the nature of *prakṛti*,
given that he too acts as the destroyer of Daityas and others in order to remove the burden of the earth.

Furthermore, since it is well-known in the Purāṇas that Rudra also protects the world by means of subduing Kālakūṭa, Andhaka, the Asuras, Tripura, and others, there would be the undesirable consequence of reversing his status as *sāttvika* and *tāmasa*. [As it is said: "O Rudra, that body of yours which is auspicious (*śivā*), not terrible (*aghorā*), and which illuminates evil..."

"O Giriśa, O Śiva, You look upon us with that most auspicious body," because this [scriptural passage] negates the *tāmasa* (dark/ignorant) nature of His body. Its meaning is as follows: O Giriśa, O Rudra, she who shines (*kāśinī*) among those free from evil (*apāpa*) is called *apāpakāśinī*.
"O you whose body brings auspicious security—expanding through that most peaceful body which is the cause of ultimate bliss, look toward us; shine forth!
For a body of darkness possesses neither non-terribleness nor the quality of being the cause of ultimate bliss."

Alternatively, it is possible that [the quality of darkness] manifests toward those who are sinless. Therefore, the body of Śiva does not possess the nature of *tamas*. If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of those Purāṇas which establish that dissolution (*saṃhāra*) is an effect of *tamas*?"
Because it has a terrible form as its object. And so says the Śruti: "Rudra indeed is that which is Agni; his are these...

The statement "He assumes two bodies, the terrible and the auspicious" is incorrect; on the contrary, it is more appropriate to say that the agency for protection and other functions belongs to Śiva alone through the medium of Viṣṇu’s body and others. Moreover, Viṣṇu’s status as having Rudra’s body is heard in scripture: "That which is his auspicious [form], when one offers the stream of clarified butter (vasordhārā)..."
By that [offering], he gratifies that body; Agni is Vasu, and this is his stream;
Viṣṇu is Vasu, and this is his stream. He offers the stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*).
Since Agni and Viṣṇu lack a body consisting of Rudra, it belongs to both those deities.
How can the body of Rudra be pleased by the oblation of *vasudhārā*, given the contradiction between what has been enjoined and its application? As it is said in the Śiva-āgama:
"O Brahman, the waters, dharma, and the moon are your terrible (*ghorā*) body; the auspicious (*śivā*) is your body."
O Brahman, [he is] Sūrya, Viṣṇu, and Hutāśana.

In this regard, it is determined that those Purāṇas and Āgamas which establish the superiority of Viṣṇu on the basis of his being the body of Śiva actually have the superiority of Śiva as their intended meaning;
for [the superiority expressed] in ornaments, hymns, and the like— which concern the superiority of the body— [pertains] to the embodied one.
Because of the final conclusion.
Now, let it be that there is a fifth [type]. In those kalpas abounding in the quality of darkness (tamas), the Purāṇas composed by Brahman characterized by that [quality] are tāmasa.

If it is argued that Śiva is also characterized by *tamas* because he is propounded therein, [we reply] that there is no evidence for the continued existence in this current Śvetavarāha-kalpa of the Purāṇas composed by Brahmā during the *tāmasa* kalpas. Even in this [present kalpa],...
For it is heard that in the twenty-eighth *kalpa*, Vyāsa composed the present-day Purāṇas. As it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"In that Vaivasvata *antara*, during the Dvāpara ages again and again, the Vedavyāsas..."
Twenty-eight have passed, O best of men.
Furthermore, the fact that Vedavyāsa, the son of Parāśara, who exists in the present, is the author of all the currently existing Purāṇas is likewise heard in the Śruti.

"He composed the Purāṇasaṃhitā, being an expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas. Having enumerated those eighteen Purāṇas in that very place, the sequence is stated according to the order of their origin: "This one indeed is named Vaiṣṇava, and the Pādma follows immediately after it."
Likewise, even regarding historical figures such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who belong to this present Kalpa,
they originate from the Lunar dynasty;
furthermore, events such as the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice caused by the daughter of Dakṣa occurred within the span of this very Kalpa.

Regarding the mutual consideration of the relative strength and weakness of the Purāṇas— composed by the twenty-eighth Vyāsa born in this Kalpa— which establish the power of the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava traditions and have been separated from one another by a vast interval of time:
The mention of the Brahmakalpas beginning with the Tāmasa is purposeless;
it must be considered how this does not induce error in the author.
[Objection: But surely the authors of the Purāṇas possess the status of being the makers of the Purāṇas...

It has been stated that [the Purāṇas] were indeed composed after learning the meanings of the Purāṇas from the presence of Brahmā. This is true; for in those cases where the Purāṇic events belong to a past kalpa, they are presented by the authors of the Purāṇas exactly as they occurred, such as the account of Mārkaṇḍeya in the Padma-kalpa.
The grace of the Supreme Lord; wherein, however, are the contents of the Purāṇas belonging to the current Kalpa, such as the incarnations of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Varāha, and so forth, or, for example,
the swallowing of the Kālakūṭa poison.
The destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice and other such events are taught by Brahmā himself as belonging specifically to this kalpa;

they are likewise presented in that same manner by the authors of the Purāṇas. Since [the author] saw no means for determining which Purāṇa was superior when faced with mutual contradictions among them, [he proceeded accordingly].
We do not know with what this presentation of the *sāttvika*, *tāmasa*, and other qualities of past eons (*kalpa*) separated by a vast period of time is consistent.

Nor is it the sixth; for although the body of Rudra, which belongs to him, is characterized by darkness (*tamas*) due to its nature as a destroyer, the Supreme Lord who possesses that body transcends it.
Thus it is said in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad:
"Having meditated upon the Lord, the Supreme Ruler, the Master, the three-eyed one, the blue-throated one, who is accompanied by Umā,
the sage goes to the source of all beings."

Although in the world the designation "tāmasa" (of the nature of darkness) is observed in common usage for Devadatta and others who possess bodies and so forth characterized primarily by the quality of *tamas*, nevertheless, the Supreme Lord— who is connected with all things— should not be understood as being qualified by that [quality] alone.

This is because the existence of many forms that transcend darkness and consist of supermundane light is established by authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, in the passage, "The multiform,
fierce, tawny one has adorned himself with firm limbs and brilliant golds," the word "brilliant" (*śubhrehi*) implies "with white [limbs]."

By the word "white" (śukla), the state of being composed of *sattva* is expressed, as in the phrase "red, white, and black. Otherwise, in the view of those who maintain the superiority of Viṣṇu, even the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas would have to be understood as teaching a Viṣṇu characterized by *tamas*.

Otherwise, there would be the consequence of [Viṣṇu] being characterized by *tamas*. How else could Viṣṇu be the destroyer of the Yādavas, Kauravas, Daityas, and others for the purpose of removing the earth's burden? Or how could he, in the form of a person named Mahāmoha, delude the Daityas in order to bewilder them?
The authorship of the scriptures by the Buddha, Jina, and others is as stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"Having been thus addressed by them, Lord Viṣṇu produced Māyāmoha from his body and gave him to the best of gods, saying this:"
This illusion, which is delusion itself, will delude all those Daityas; consequently, having been cast outside the path of the Vedas, they shall become fit for bondage.

For indeed, when there is the presence of great delusion (*mahāmoha*), there is no other well-known material cause (*upādāna*) for one's own darkness (*tamas*) than that very [delusion], by which the state of being characterized by *tamas* in one's own body would not exist. Now, [one might object] regarding Viṣṇu...

For the sake of his specific function, although he possesses the quality of *tamas*, it is not predominant because it is overwhelmed by *sattva*. In the case of Rudra, however, both *sattva* and *rajas* are overwhelmed by *tamas*;
thus, *tamas* is predominant, and he is characterized as the agent of dissolution and so forth due to being distinguished by that [quality].
"Let the seventh position—that it is the state of being the object to be propounded—be accepted. Not so;

for in the case of incarnations such as Nṛsiṃha, whose sole purpose is the destruction of enemies, there would follow the consequence of their being predominantly *tāmasa*, and thus Śiva would possess the nature of consisting of *tamas*.

Furthermore, [the first alternative] is untenable because it is contradicted by the very position [of the opponent]. Nor is the latter [alternative] correct. As for that tamasic agent who performs the dissolution, does he himself have some dissolver or not? If he does, then despite being tamasic, he alone would be the most supreme, because of his independence in performing the dissolution of all things. If he does not, then this [very one under discussion] is [the supreme agent].

The reason "because he is the destroyer of all" is contradictory, for being *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness) is pervaded by being subordinate to all; thus, [the claim] that Rudra is superior to all because he is the destroyer of all is a contradictory probans (*viruddha-hetu*). Therefore, Rudra is superior to all because he is the destroyer of all, as opposed to the individual soul (*jīva*) in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Nor is this reason unestablished (*aprayojaka*).

This is the reason: because the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is impossible without a distinction between strength and weakness; because being sattvic is pervaded by the state of being sublated, which is contradictory to [the power of] destruction; and according to the maxim that "that which is weak is everywhere sublated."

Nor is there a lack of establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*), because it is established within the very subject (*pakṣa*) itself, namely, "Rudra is superior to the universe. Since the inference is for the purpose of bestowing grace upon him, there is no fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*).
In this manner, being *sāttvika* should be analyzed and refuted according to the aforementioned method.

Now, it may be argued that the Purāṇas are characterized as *sāttvika* because they primarily propound Viṣṇu, who is dominated by the quality of *sattva*, and that Viṣṇu himself possesses a predominance of *sattva*. As stated in the Bhāgavata: "Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of Prakṛti; the Supreme Person here is indeed associated with them."
(51) He bears [these names]; for indeed, the names Hari, Viriñci, and Hara denote creation and the rest, and therein lie the highest blessings.
If it is argued that [the qualities] of sattva, rajas, and tamas belong to men according to their bodies, as is heard regarding Viṣṇu, we say no;

for this would entail the consequence that the Purāṇas such as the Mārkaṇḍeya, which establish the superiority of Viṣṇu, are of the nature of *sāttvika*, while those establishing the superiority of Rudra [would be otherwise].

Because it would follow that the *Padma Purāṇa* and others are characterized by *tamas*. If you argue that since the *Padma Purāṇa* describes the superiority of both Hari and Hara through its Pūrva- and Uttara-khaṇḍas, its *tāmasa* nature is accepted only in those specific parts, [we reply] that the same applies to the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Bhāgavata*, and so forth.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being insentient (*tāmasa*). In the *Bālakāṇḍa* of the *Rāmāyaṇa*:

"O King, I see no one other than the wielder of the trident—Umā’s husband, Paśupati, who is honored by all the worlds—who is capable of bearing that [missile]. This same weapon is also mentioned in the *Yuddhakāṇḍa*.

"Whether it be my terrible power or that of Vāryambaka. Furthermore, in the Uttarakāṇḍa, there is an extensive description of the confinement of Rāvaṇa at his residence on Kailāsa, the subjugation of Rāvaṇa, the favor shown to Indrajit, and so forth; and likewise regarding the destruction of Rāvaṇa.
Because of the description of [the mountain] being caused by Rudra’s disregard,
then, O Rāma, Mahādeva, laughing at what he had done, playfully pressed that mountain with his big toe. Then, being thus oppressed there—
The arms reached down to the base of the mountain.
Once again, in that very place—
that linga adorned with various jewels shone forth— after Rāvaṇa had worshipped that deity, he proceeded according to his custom.
All that is accomplished for him who does not worship Hara;
however, this evil-minded Rāvaṇa acts with contempt when [the ritual is performed].
At that time, the death of this person is contemplated by the sages and the deities; yet he, being intoxicated,
does not realize that his worship of Śiva is devoid of the prescribed ritual.

In this way, it should be seen in many ways that even for Indrajit, who was the cause of Rama’s defeat on numerous occasions while accompanied by the monkey army, the granting of boons and other favors were performed by Maheśvara; thus, the superiority of Śiva is to be observed. Likewise, in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, regarding the immortality of Bāṇāsura—

The granting of boons and so forth should also be understood in this light. Nor is it appropriate to claim that even this [text], which establishes the superiority of Śiva, is characterized by *tamas* (ignorance/darkness), because it contradicts the words of Brahmā: "Not a single word of yours shall ever be untrue in this poem. Thus it is stated in the *Bhāgavata*.
In the fourth book, in the dialogue between Aditi and Kaśyapa: "He who has neither kinsman nor stranger in the world,
whom no one holds in high esteem and whom no one censures— he, O Jambavat, we desire as our husband, once he has cast off his vows and enjoyed his pleasures."

The conduct of that wise one was beyond reproach, and those who discerned it were repelled by the veil of ignorance within the home; he himself, though naturally devoid of both equality and superiority, practiced the behavior of a *piśāca*, for such is the way of the virtuous.
For the unfortunate laugh at the desired conduct of that wise one who has remembered his true self,
just as they would laugh at food [eaten] with clothes, garlands, ornaments, and ointments, because it is regarded as their own self.
Praised by Brahmā and the other gods, he for whom the guardians of the bridge were appointed, and by whose cause this entire universe is sustained like snow.
Even the practice of a Piśāca is obedient to him; oh, how the conduct of the All-pervading Lord is a mockery!
(53) With a mass of matted hair grey with the dust and smoke from the winds of the cremation ground’s fire,
his stainless golden body smeared with ashes— the god beholds you, O goddess, with three eyes.
Nor are these [scriptures] characterized by *tamas* (darkness) by virtue of their establishing Śiva;

for the first verse [establishes Him] as "the unborn source of those who have experienced enjoyment," the second as "than whom there is nothing higher or more supreme," and the third as "everything rests in His stability."

Because [the view that Viṣṇu is] "established" would involve a state of tamasic nature, being consistent in meaning with such Vedic passages as, "He who in the beginning created Brahmā," and because it would follow that those texts establishing the superiority of Viṣṇu would lack authority due to this contradiction.

In the section concerning the non-occurrence of Smṛti (*smṛty-anavakāśādhikaraṇa*), the statements of the Purāṇas and Āgamas—which accord with direct Vedic revelation and establish the preeminence of Śiva—are contrasted with the statements of the Smṛtis of Manu and others, which have their basis in directly perceived Veda;
[the same logic applies to] the Sāṃkhya Smṛti... [and so forth].

This is because it is logical that such [texts] would subvert statements from the Matsya Purāṇa, the Kūrma Purāṇa, and others which establish the superiority of Viṣṇu, just as the *dhak* syllable subverts other sounds. By this, even the specific enumeration of the Sāttvika and other classes of Purāṇas is refuted.
For, by counting Rudra as superior even among the Sāttvika Purāṇas which you yourself have enumerated, your own enumeration becomes futile. Thus it was said by you:
"The Brahmāṇḍa, the Brahmakaivarta, and likewise the Mārkaṇḍeya..."
Listen now to the future Vāmana incarnation, which is Brāhma; next, learn of those that are Rājasa.
Know that these six— the Mātsya, Kaurma, Liṅga, Vāyavīya, Skānda, and Āgneya Purāṇas— are characterized by tamas.
O lady of auspicious appearance, the Vaiṣṇava, Nāradīya, the auspicious Bhāgavata, Gāruḍa, Pādma, and Vārāha are the Sāttvika Purāṇas that bestow liberation.
These auspicious [deeds] are declared to be rajasic and bestow heaven.

"Those which are *tāmasa* lead to hell. Thus, if Brahmāṇu and Vāmana were *rājasa*, then because the greatness of the Raṅga within them and the greatness of Veṅkaṭācala would also be *rājasa*, they would not bestow liberation. This is according to the verse beginning with "Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas... (Bhagavad Gītā 14.5).

Since *sattva* is a quality of *prakṛti*, Viṣṇu, being endowed with it, would also be *prākṛta* (derived from *prakṛti*). And thus the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The state of being *sāttvika* is pervaded by *prākṛtatva* (the state of being derived from *prakṛti*), because it resides exclusively in that which is distinct from [the states of] *sāttvika* and so forth, just like the state of being *tāmasa*. Nor is this [the case].

The statement that "the Blessed One resorts to pure *sattva* during his maintenance" would otherwise be contradictory; for the meaning of the term "pure" (*viśuddha*) is precisely that which is not overcome by the other [qualities]. By this, the modern view that he resorts to *prakṛta-sattva* (material *sattva*) is refuted. It is *aprākṛta* (non-material).

For there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that *rajas* and *tamas* would also possess [the power of] accomplishment (*siddhi*). Therefore, the reason is not "inconclusive" (*aprayojaka*). And thus, Śiva transcends the *guṇas* because he transcends *prakṛti*, like a liberated soul (*muktapuruṣa*). There is neither inconclusiveness nor lack of proof (*asiddhatva*) [in this argument], since for him who was merged in *prakṛti*, that which...
The phrase "the supreme Maheśvara" contradicts the Śruti which establishes that [Maheśvara] is beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

In this way, the *Matsya Purāṇa* passage beginning with "and of Śiva among the tāmasas," etc., is also refuted; for you yourself have included the *Matsya Purāṇa* among the *tāmasa* texts, and thus this statement [of yours]—

Because there is a contradiction between the two authorities; for if the Matsya Purāṇa is included among the Tāmasa texts in order to establish that Śiva is Tāmasa... [p. 55] ...then there is a conflict.

In that matter, it is the authoritative source (*pramāṇa*). This is because the same logic applies. Otherwise, the authority of the speaker of that Purāṇa—the one in the form of the Fish—would be compromised;
furthermore, the retrieval of the Vedas and other acts performed by the Fish Incarnation would likewise become utterly purposeless.
It would become highly confused, because the suspicion of unreliability (*anāptatva*) is easily found everywhere.
In this way, even the *Kūrma Purāṇa* must be justified according to the principle already stated.
If the *Śaiva* and other *Purāṇas* were to be considered *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness) simply because they propound Śiva, [then the same logic would apply].

In that case, since there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the various textual compositions— such as the Vedic passages directly teaching that [deity], beginning with "Obeisance to you, O Rudra" and "Subtler than the subtle"— being characterized as *tāmasa* (dark/ignorant),
it is more appropriate for those who accept authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) to exclude them from the Veda altogether. By this [it is shown that...]
The claim that the Śaiva Āgamas and Purāṇas, which establish the superiority of Śiva,

are delusive scriptures (*mohaśāstra*) has also been refuted; for [if that were so], it would follow that even the Lord himself— who says, "I create this delusion"— would be untrustworthy, since he speaks of things he himself has taught.
Because it would result in the Pāñcarātra Āgamas being rendered invalid;
for, in reality, the superiority of Śiva is established by direct Vedic revelation (śruti) and other authorities,
whereas the Itihāsas and Purāṇas favored by you are merely characterized as "sāttvika" (pure).
Because it has been shown to be that which corroborates [the Vedas],

and because those Purāṇas and Āgamas that contradict it are sublated by the principles established in the *Virodhādhikaraṇa* and the *Smṛty-anavakāśa* [sūtras], the superiority of Śiva is established without hindrance.

But is it not said that Śiva is beyond the *guṇas* and therefore not characterized by *tamas*? That is incorrect, because he is a slayer of Brahmā due to his severing the fifth head of the four-faced one.
As it is said in the Vāmana Purāṇa:
"Having heard that, the high-souled Śaṅkara, filled with wrath, [struck] with the tip of his nail..."
The head of Brahmā was severed by one who spoke harsh words.
That severed head fell upon the very palm of Śaṅkara’s left hand; indeed, that head never fell from the hand of Śaṅkara.

Nor is it logical to say that there is no *brahmahatyā* (the sin of killing a Brahmin) simply because Brahmā is not subject to death; for it is said: "Then, having emerged from him, the fierce *Brahmahatyā*, with the luster of a mass of black collyrium, terrifying with her blood-red hair, approached Hara."
"I have arrived as the murder of a Brahmin; accept me, O Three-eyed One!"—having spoken these words, the Brahmin-murder entered him.
"Rudra, who holds a trident in his hand... and so forth; for this is heard in that very [text].
And likewise, the state of being a skull-bearer (*kapālitva*) is also heard in that very same place:
"Thus, O divine sage, he became known as Kapālī, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes; for this reason, he [is so called]."
He was not invited by Dakṣa.

Therefore, how can there be the killing of a Brahmin and the wearing of a Brahmin’s skull by Śiva, who is supreme over all? It is said in response: in the passage "Because he consumes the moving and the unmoving," it is stated that "both the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya become his food. Thus, the Brahmin...

The power of destruction belonging to the Supreme Lord, who consumes everything including the Kṣatriyas and others, is indeed a virtue; thus, the delusion regarding virtue and defect belongs only to those who [do not understand] the causes. Furthermore, the incurrence of the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) through the decapitation of Dakṣa, a consecrated (*dīkṣita*) Brāhmaṇa engaged in sacrifice, is recorded in the Purāṇas.

It has not been heard [in scripture]: even though the ego was removed by the cutting off of Brahmā’s fifth head, how was the killing of Brahmā reckoned as occurring while he was still alive? For it is an action intended for death and resulting in death that constitutes *hiṃsā* (violence).

For if there is an absence of resulting in death, there is an absence of the nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*). Therefore, it is for this very reason that the common worldly usage treats acts such as the *śyena* sacrifice— which is prescribed with the intent of the enemy's death— as being of the nature of violence.

This applies to those who follow the Vedas. For this very reason, there is the conventional designation of "non-violent" for one who digs a well, because his action is not intended to cause death. Likewise, even if no living being is killed by an iron arrow shot with the intent to kill, the shooter is not conventionally designated as "violent."

Because it lacks the result of death; nor does the severing of Brahmā’s head have death as its intended purpose, since its objective is solely the dispelling of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). As it is said in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*:
Then, having seen the faces of Bhava out of delusion, the face of Pitāmaha spoke these words:
"Are there any supreme powers in those bubbles that arise from this struck water?"
Having heard that, the high-souled Śaṅkara, filled with wrath, severed with the tip of his nail the head of the Brahmā who had spoken so harshly;
for if death were intended, it would have been possible to cut off even another head.

Because there is no prohibitor [of such an act], and because its purpose is merely the removal of the letter "A" (aṃkāra), it lacks the intent of death; therefore, it cannot be classified as violence (*hiṃsā*). For even in the Purāṇas, the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) is not described in the case of Dakṣa's sacrifice. Brahman...

Because the quality of being the destroyer of the entire world, including the Kṣatriyas and others, is a proof of his status as Īśvara; and because for Rudra—who is the destroyer of the infinite four-faced Brahmās residing within many kalpas and cosmic eggs—the designation of being a "slayer of Brahman" (brahmahantṛ) is actually an ornament [of his majesty]. Now, [it may be asked: "Did she not come from there?"
If it is asked, "What is the purpose of the statement regarding the attainment of the terrible sin of killing a Brahmin?
[the answer is: it refers to that sacred field of Kāśī. (p. 58)
Because it is intended as a praise for the purpose of establishing the power to avert the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), it is so stated in the Vāmana Purāṇa in that very context:
"O Great-minded Lord of the Gods, in such a place as Vārāṇasī; having gone there..."

"O best of gods, you shall obtain liberation from sin. Now, one might object: since it is said, "Having touched a human corpse, one should enter the water while still wearing one's clothes, [as the body consists of] bones and sinews," the skull is impure; therefore, its wearing would result in a state of ritual impurity. If this is the objection:
Not so; for that [text] has another purpose, namely, to establish the majesty of the sacred ford (tīrtha) called Kapālamocana located in Kāśī. And thus it is said in that very place:
"The sage, having bathed at Kapālamocana according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas..."
As Tripurāntaka was bathing at that sacred ford (tīrtha), the skull fell from the palm of his hand. Then, by the grace of the Blessed One, that excellent tīrtha became known by the name Kapālamocana.
Consequently, Rudra shall become renowned in the world as Kapālī.

Even though he has abandoned the skull, his renown as a "Skull-bearer" (Kapālin) is established because it serves as a cause for excellence, indicating his superiority over Brahmā and others; otherwise, even Viṣṇu would [be so designated],
as he too possesses the bone from the head of the Daitya named Pañcajana.
By holding the *pāñcajanya*, impurity would arise. As it is said in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*:
"O destroyer of demons, the Daityas named Pañcajana seized the children who were in the form of the conch [Pāñcajanya] within my waters."
When this was said, Kṛṣṇa went into the water, slew that Pañcajana,
and took from his bones that supreme conch-shell, the source [of its sound].
"Having filled that Pāñcajanya [conch]... (as in the passage on p.
59), and likewise, by the killing of Rāvaṇa and the consecration of Rāmeśvara at the Setu, [the sin of] killing a Brahmin [was purified].
Furthermore, since the description of its cessation is seen extensively in the Purāṇas, this fault is equal for others as well; for instance, in the thirty-first chapter of the Āditya Purāṇa:
"Having installed Mahādeva in the middle of the Setu, that Rāghava obtained..."
Through the grace of Śiva, the Lord, [he attained] supreme devotion.
Mahādeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, is renowned as Rāmeśvara;
by the mere sight of him, even the sin of killing a Brahmin is dispelled.
Regarding the sin of killing a woman due to the slaying of Bhṛgu’s wife, it is stated in the Rāmāyaṇa:
"O Rāma, in ancient times, the mother of Kāvya, the wife of Bhṛgu who was firm in her vows, was slain by Viṣṇu because she desired a world without Indra."
If those [scriptural passages] have another purpose, the same resolution applies here as well.

In reality, however, because the Supreme Lord is omniscient, there is no stain of connection with sin; likewise, for individual souls who possess knowledge of reality, the absence of such stain is described. And so says the Sūtra:
"In the case of ascending that [ladder], there is the non-attachment to and destruction of future and past sins, because of the designation thereof.

By this, the eating of the skull-fragments is also explained; for the filling of the Pāñcajanya conch is impossible without its connection to the mouth. Likewise, the wandering for alms is like the theft of butter and so forth.

Because he was in a state of meditative absorption (*samāhita*). In reality, however, the severing of Brahmā’s head and the carrying of that skull were performed by Bhairava—known as Saṃhārarudra—who is a portion of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) and is dominated by the quality of darkness (*tamas*). Thus, it is not [the case that Śiva acted out of passion].

The Supreme Lord’s state of being a skull-bearer or his [committing] the murder of a Brahmin is likewise [described]. Thus, at the beginning [of the text]: "In that same way, another [form] consisting of darkness arose, three-eyed, holding a trident in his hand, with matted hair, displaying a rosary of beads."
"Rudra, enveloped by egoism, replied to the Grandfather," so it is said.
And in the conclusion: "I am indeed this embodiment of darkness, a portion of you, born of wrath.
Nor is there a lack of evidence for a Supreme Lord beyond this; for it is said in the *Tāpanīya*:
They consider the fourth to be non-dual, auspicious, and peaceful, whose essence is the cognition of the one Self; thus,
because Śiva is designated as "the fourth" in relation to Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu, the employment of seven terms denoting Śiva— such as *Śambhu*, *Śaṅkara*, and so forth— is untenable.

For it is possible to apply terms such as "Śiva" to [the individual soul] through its being a portion of Śiva (*śivāṃśa*) and through its similarity to Him, just as the term "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*) is applied [to a servant]. For this very reason, one who disregards the attribution of skull-bearingness (*kapālitva*), which resides in Saṃhārarudra, to the Supreme Lord...
We consider it logical that Dakṣa, due to the delusion of his egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), became subject to restraint by the hosts of Vīrabhadra and others. As it has been said:
"Thus he became Kapālī, O divine sage," and so forth. [The three fires...]
He gazed at Dakṣa with his three eyes; as soon as he was seen by the Three-eyed One, he was reduced to ashes in an instant.

And in the Kāśīkhaṇḍa, this [state] is described as belonging to Bhairava himself, who is a portion (aṃśa) of Rudra; this dialogue should be consulted. Thus, the Supreme Lord is untainted (nirlepa) because he possesses knowledge of reality and because he is omniscient, like a liberated soul (muktātman).
Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Lord is superior to all.
Now, how is Sadāśiva superior to others? (p.
61) Because the fruit resulting from the worship of those [others] is unstable, whereas for Daśagrīva and others, [the fruit] resulted from the worship of Śiva.
Because his sovereignty is more renowned [than that of others]. Thus it has been said:

"Having effortlessly brought the three worlds under his control, free from the interference of enemies, the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), whose arms were itching for battle, [filled] the quarters with the lotuses of his heads..."
This is the manifestation of the Destroyer of Tripura, arising from your firm devotion to the lotus-feet of Balarāma.

Because one observes the destruction of the sovereignty of others— such as that of the Daityas and Dānavas— who likewise obtained their power through the grace of Śiva, it follows that the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) bestows unstable boons. In contrast, [the sovereignty] of Nārāyaṇa, however, was attained by Dhruva, Vibhīṣaṇa, and others [and is eternal].

The intention of others is that He alone is the supreme among all, because He bestows the most excellent and most stable sovereignty as well as liberation; thus, He is the giver of the most stable boon. In this regard, it is asked: is the fruit of karma unstable? Or rather...

The fruit of knowledge as well [is not liberation]. Not the first [alternative], because it has been established—by such scriptural passages as "Just as here the world acquired through action perishes"—that sovereignty over heaven and so forth is impermanent, a fact accepted by all.
Nor the second: [for it is said,] "Having known the Lord, one becomes immortal."
They exist because the direct realization of Īśvara is the cause of imperishable liberation (*mokṣa*).

If it is argued that even though the fruit of ritual action (*karma-phala*) is impermanent, the worship of Viṣṇu has as its fruit a state lasting until the end of a kalpa, whereas the worship of Sadāśiva does not— this is not so.
For even through the worship of Śiva, infinite sovereignty is attained by Bāṇāsura, Sukeśin, Nandīśvara, and others; as it is stated in the Vāmana Purāṇa:
In this place, there is a lord of the night-stalkers known as Vidhutkeśin;
though Īśāna was pleased with him, he [granted] a city that moves through the sky.
He granted him invincibility against enemies as well as immunity from being slain;
and in the *Uttara-rāmāyaṇa*:
"Having made him truly immortal, the great god Mahādeva—immutable and undecaying—"
Out of a desire to please Umā, he gave her a city that travels through the sky.

Then, O King, having obtained the favor of the Goddess and his lord Hara, the high-minded Sukeśin, arrogant from the granting of that boon, traversed the entire earth like Purandara reaching the city of the birds (Amarāvatī).

Likewise, regarding the granting of immortality to the Asura Bāṇa, it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "O Lord, this immunity from fear has been granted by me to this Bāṇa; even though he has provoked us, O Imperishable One, he is not to be slain by you."
In the *Bhārata*, at the time when Arjuna was granted the *Pāśupatāstra* by Īśvara, [the latter] bestowed liberation upon him.
If it is asked, "How then can the sovereignty of Rāvaṇa be unstable?", we reply that it is because of *dharma* in the form of contempt for the Supreme Lord. And so says Nandikeśvara:
In the *Uttara-Rāmāyaṇa*, the curse directed toward Rāvaṇa is as follows:
there, the venerable Nandin, an alternative manifestation (*aparā tanu*) of Śaṅkara, being enraged, spoke to that ten-faced Rākṣasa standing there: "Since you [assumed] the form of a monkey..."
O Daśānana, disregarding me, he let out a loud laugh resembling the crash of a thunderbolt.
"Therefore, monkeys resembling my own face, possessing my prowess and equal to me in splendor, shall be born for the sake of slaying you and this entire race.
Thus did the Lord grant a trident to Madhu, the Daitya who was the father of the Asura Lavaṇa.
At that time, he was made to fear the violation of dharma. And so it is said in the *Uttararāmāyaṇa*:
"This incomparable, auspicious dharma of yours brings me favor, by which..."
Being pleased, I then give you this supreme weapon, the slayer of enemies.
As long as he does not create enmity with the gods and the brahmins, so long shall this [kingdom] be yours;
otherwise, it will go to destruction.
In this way, even for the Asura Andhaka, there was the granting of a boon by the Supreme Lord as well as a limit regarding its violation of Dharma.
Likewise, in the Vāmana Purāṇa, there is the statement of Prahlāda:
"O Dānava, Mahādeva was propitiated here by your son as well, who was ever devoted to Dharma."
Having thus spoken these words to the one desiring a son, the Lord said: "But when he performs a wicked deed that is loathed by the world, [he shall obtain his desire]."
If he should cause a Brahmin to be killed, or hate all the gods,
then I myself shall here undergo the emaciation of his body.

Otherwise, even for Viṣṇu, there would be the fault of granting unstable boons, because his bestowing of sovereignty upon the Yādavas and Kauravas—such as Yudhiṣṭhira and Ugrasena—as well as upon Kucela, Sāndīpani, and others, was transient. This has been stated by him [Viṣṇu] himself: "To whomsoever I desire to show favor..."
"I shall take away his wealth.

However, in reality, because the Supreme Lord is the presiding authority over dharma, he grants boons only in a manner that does not contradict dharma; as stated in the sūtra *phalamata upapatteḥ* (The fruit [of action comes] from Him, because it is logical).

Since the word "fruit" (phala) is common to both pleasure and pain, just as the Supreme Lord, being pleased by austerity, grants a boon that is a cause of happiness, so too the Supreme Lord, being displeased by prohibited action, [bestows its fruit].

[The Lord] bestows the suffering of hell and other realms. Just as one dispels evil through dharma, so too does one dispel merit through adharma. Thus, the Supreme Lord alone is the giver of the fruit.

It is established that because the sin produced by Rāvaṇa and others' lust for the wives of others overcomes their merit characterized by austerity, their destruction is appropriately very swift; thus, there is no loss of the Supreme Lord's preeminence.
Is it not true that Viṣṇu alone is the supreme among all? For when Gajendra offered praise to the primordial source, the Supreme Brahman, and sought refuge in the ultimate cause,
Nārāyaṇa himself manifested before him in order to protect his devotee who had surrendered.

He liberated him from the snare of the crocodile; others, such as Brahmā and the rest, did not manifest themselves to protect him. Likewise, in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, at the beginning of the hymn by Gajendra:
I take refuge in that self-existent one, in whom this [universe] exists, from whom this [universe] arises, by whom this [universe] is pervaded,
who himself is this [universe], and who is higher than both this [empirical world] and the other [transcendental reality].

And in the conclusion: "Thus, Brahmā and the others, who possess the conceit of various distinctions among their respective emblems, did not approach Gajendra as he was described— that is, [the Lord] who is non-differentiated [from him], because He is the Self of all."
There, Hari appeared, composed of all the immortals.

Therefore, when the praise of the Supreme Being was being performed by Gajendra, he who protected him is indeed the Supreme Being; for it is not the case that he who protected him while the refuge was sought in another is the Supreme Being. It is another.

It is logical that he "protects. Therefore, although it might be argued that Nārāyaṇa is the supreme among all, we reply: even though the praise by Gajendra was directed specifically toward the Supreme Cause (p.
And although such practice was performed, nevertheless, because Nārāyaṇa is authorized for the protection of the world, it is proper that he should provide that protection;
for when someone is oppressed by calamities and the like and utters a cry of distress directed toward the king, [the king must respond].

It is logical that protection is provided by a minister for a king, because he is authorized for that task of protection. However, the Supreme Lord Viṣṇu is not authorized for the protection [of others], as stated in the Anuśāsanika Parva.
That very Lord Rudra, the imperishable source of all principles and the like,
created from his right limb Brahmā, the originator of the worlds.
Likewise, for the sake of protecting the world, the Lord [created] Viṣṇu;
and [this was stated] by Jaimini in the Veda-pāda-stava.

"By whose command Nārāyaṇa stands pervading the entire universe. And in the Yajurveda: "They say that from Vāta comes the strength of Viṣṇu. According to the logic of the *Prāṇādhikaraṇa*, the meaning is: "They say that the strength of Viṣṇu comes from the Supreme Lord who is denoted by the word Vāta."

Alternatively, since the lordly elephant was a devotee of Viṣṇu in his previous birth, it is logical that when he offered praise to Viṣṇu alone as the Supreme Brahman, Viṣṇu alone was pleased and no other. And so it is said in the Bhāgavata:
He who was formerly the king of Pāṇḍya, the best of the Draviḍas, known as Indradyumna,
was devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu.
"By the power of his worship of Hari, he possessed such recollection even while in the state of an elephant. Thus it is said.
And in the Gītā:
"O son of Kuntī, declare it: my devotee perishes not.
I am their deliverer from death, from the ocean of saṃsāra.

Furthermore, is Viṣṇu’s praise as the Supreme Brahman itself the proof for his being the Supreme Brahman, or is it the impossibility of his not departing [from this world] immediately after such praise? It cannot be the first, because praise—like the statement "All this is indeed water" and so forth—is not a means of establishing reality. It cannot be the second...

The second [reason] is that protecting one's own devotees, like protecting one's own sons and servants, serves as a means for attaining the Supreme Brahman; or else, it is because the protection of Gajendra is justified by his qualification for protection [as a devotee]. In the Vāmana Purāṇa, however, there is mention of Gajendra’s many births.
From that time forward, his devotion to Viṣṇu and his practice of praising Viṣṇu became clearly manifest. Being afflicted by disease, devoid of energy, seized by a terrible affliction,
and having fallen into supreme calamity, he meditated upon Hari in his mind.
He was a glorious devotee of the Lord, solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa; through the practice of many successive births, he possessed devotion for the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
He worshipped no other god than Mahādeva, namely Keśava,
the lotus-navelled one who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
And a hymn was offered:
"Homage to Govinda, the foundation of the world; homage again and again! Homage be to Padmanābha, and to him who is the source of Sāṃkhya and Yoga! Thus it was said.

Furthermore, the praise of Viṣṇu is clearly understood; therefore, it is concluded that it was Viṣṇu himself who arrived for the protection of his own devotee. However, this much does not establish the superiority of that arrival over all others; so, enough with excessive elaboration.

Now, how is it that Śiva’s supremacy over all is established? When he had granted a boon to the demon named Bhasmāsura— a former Vṛkāsura— and when that demon began to place [the boon] upon his head with his hand—
Because he protected [the world] from Nārāyaṇa while it was fleeing from all the worlds, it is said in the tenth book of the *Bhāgavata*, in the eighty-seventh chapter:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others are masters over anger and grace; [yet they were powerless] against Vṛkāsura..."
Having granted the boon, Giriśa emerged from the peril.
From the god, that most wicked one chose a boon that brought fear to all beings: "Whosoever I place my hand upon the head, let him die."
In order to test that boon, the asura indeed began to place his own hand upon the head of Śambhu,
and he ran about in all directions.
Thus, his mind pierced by the Lord’s various and elegant words of praise,
the dull-witted one was struck with wonder and placed his own hand upon his head.

Then, with his head shattered as if struck by a thunderbolt in an instant, [he fell]. Furthermore, since even Bhṛgu and others have reached the certainty that Viṣṇu is superior, Viṣṇu alone is indeed the most eminent.
This has been stated in that very same place:
On the lovely bank of the Sarasvatī, the sages were performing a sacrificial session (sattra). A deliberation arose among them as to which of the three [Vedas] was the greatest.
Desiring to know that [truth], O King, they sent Bhrigu, the son of Brahmā, to him for the sake of his instruction;
he then went to the assembly of Brahmā.
He did not offer praise to that Brahmā, testing his true nature;
at this, the Blessed One became enraged, blazing with his own splendor.
Then he went to Kailāsa, where the god Maheśvara rose up with joy and began to embrace his brother.
"He does not wish to go on the wrong path," the god said, and he became enraged; with eyes turned fierce, he raised his trident and began to strike him down.
Falling at his feet, the queen consoled him with her words;
then she went to Vaikuṇṭha, where the god Janārdana resides.
Striking him on the chest with his foot as he lay upon the lap of Śrī,
the Blessed One, the refuge of the seven worlds, then rose up together with Lakṣmī.
Then, descending from his own couch, he bowed his head to the sage;
hearing that, the sages were struck with wonder and their doubts were dispelled.
They placed greater faith in Viṣṇu, from whom comes peace and from whom comes fearlessness.
And because it bestows dispassion: "I shall gradually take away the wealth of that person whom I favor;
then his own kinsmen will abandon him as if he were miserable. I shall grant my grace to one who has performed the mantra dedicated to me.
In the Brahmakāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa: "The gods, along with the hosts of sages, regarded Viṣṇu as superior even to Brahmā."
And the Śruti says:
"Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Reality.
Therefore, because He subdued the demon Vṛka, who brought fear even to Rudra, by Bhṛgu and the others—

Since it is determined that Viṣṇu alone is superior due to his supreme tranquility and because he manifested his power in battle, and since he alone is also the Supreme Reality (paratattva), this being the position reached, we reply: Śiva alone is the Supreme Reality. He who is the first among the gods, at their head—Rudra, who is superior to the dual [Viṣṇu and Brahmā].
The Great Sage [says]: Because of the two Upaniṣadic statements, "There is nothing higher than Him" and "There is nothing else whatsoever," any reality superior to Rudra is negated.
Nor is it unestablished that these two [statements] form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), for they both culminate in the same action.

It must be stated that, because of the expectancy regarding the division [of the referent], the pronoun [functions] as in the case of "I prepare a pleasant seat for you; sit upon it" and "he returns to immortality. (p. 69) Thus, due to the expectancy in the context of the division, the pronoun [is connected].

This is because it refers back to what was previously mentioned in the context. As it has been said: "A pronoun [serves] to indicate a well-known object or to bring about the understanding of an unknown object; when it depends on what is well-known, it draws down [the meaning] from that which stands in the preceding sentence."
